results.requestText: What should I wear to work tomorrow?

looks.title: Check Blazer, Finally Worn
looks.idea: A rust-and-brown check blazer over stripes, sharpened with a belted waist.
looks.howToWear: Tuck the Breton top into the navy cigarette trousers and put the wide black belt at your natural waist. Wear the oversized blazer open with the sleeves pushed up just to the wrist bone. The slim cropped trouser keeps the proportions balanced under the boyfriend-fit jacket. Add the gold hoops and carry the black tote. Wear the camel coat over the top for the walk and the Tube.
looks.why: This is the one piece you haven't yet found a use for, and it makes a strong pitch-ready jacket. The rust and cream in the check warm up the navy stripe, and print-on-print is your signature. The slim trouser and belt mark your waist so the oversized blazer doesn't swamp you, which is the lesson from the tulle and cable-knit day. Black Chelsea boots are fine in drizzle, and your arms stay covered. It's polished without the default black blazer.

looks.title: Pink Tweed and Florals
looks.idea: Colour-on-colour joy with one sharp, cropped jacket.
looks.howToWear: Tuck the cobalt merino into the high-rise floral wide-leg trousers so the waist is clear. Put the cropped pink tweed jacket over it, worn open, and let the hem sit right at your waistline. Pull the trousers up so the hems skim the top of the red Mary Janes. Add the gold hoops, a few bangles over the jumper cuff, and the red mini bag. The belted trench goes over the top for drizzle.
looks.why: This repeats your navy floral and cobalt combination, which felt joyful, and adds the tweed jacket you've worn only once. The pink picks up the pink in the trousers. The cropped jacket and high rise suit your waist and short-legged proportions. The tweed gives the outfit a sharp, polished element for the office. Cobalt and red are in your best colours, and your arms are fully covered.

looks.title: Baroque Wrap, Dressed Down for Drizzle
looks.idea: Your most-complimented dress, made sharp and weatherproof for the office.
looks.howToWear: Wear the wrap dress with the black opaque tights and the flat knee-high boots, with the hem falling at or just over the boot tops so the leg line stays unbroken. Wear the burgundy beret slightly back off the face. Add the gold hoops and stacked bangles. Wear the belted trench over the dress, cinched tight, and carry the black tote.
looks.why: The wrap dress is already your most flattering piece, with a defined waist, long sleeves and a polished formality of 4/5, so it handles a client pitch without any extra effort. Dark tights and boots in the same colour make your legs look longer. The beret picks up the burgundy in the print and keeps your hair dry in the drizzle. The black stays at the feet and the coat, away from your face. Leather boots and a water-resistant trench suit a wet commute.

output.note: I left the black tailored blazer in the wardrobe on purpose, since each look here has a more interesting sharp element. Avoid the tan suede boots tomorrow because of the drizzle.

failures.detail: m45 rust/brown check + m06 navy Breton + m27 navy + m60/m85/m71 black + m50 camel has no warm bright anywhere. It reads as French-girl menswear, not colour-forward Dries/Susie Bubble. Stripe-with-check is a print mix, but a muted one.

A hip-length boyfriend blazer cuts her at the widest, lowest point and shortens already-short legs. The m85 belt is mostly hidden by the open jacket. Layering the oversized m45 under the below-knee m50 also bunches through the sleeves.

Calling it 'pitch-ready' and saying the rust 'warms up the navy' are assertions, not visual reasons. The tulle/cable-knit lesson was about volume top AND bottom, which a slim trouser fixes, but the hip-length cut problem is not addressed.

looks.comment: Getting the never-worn m45 out is the right instinct, and the stripe-under-check mix is credible. But this is the most restrained thing she could do with it. Swap m06 for m01 leopard blouse or m10 cobalt merino, and add m84 scarf at the neck, and it becomes hers.

failures.detail: m74 red mini shoulder bag won't carry a work day's kit; she needs the m71 tote as a second bag. Full-length crepe m20 wide-legs over m62 flats will wick up drizzle on a walk-and-Tube commute. 'Pull the trousers up' is not possible on a high-rise and should be dropped.
The m51 black trench collar does sit at her face, which contradicts the colouring note. It's a commute layer, but say so.

looks.comment: This is the strongest look, and exactly her: m42 cropped at the waist over high-rise m20 is the ideal proportion for her short-legged hourglass. Pink, cobalt and red with gold is Susie Bubble done with polish. It builds on a proven hit and wakes up a once-worn jacket.

failures.detail: m87 burgundy beret with a black belted trench and black knee boots tips toward a Parisian cliché. It also does little against drizzle, despite the claim. Keep it optional.
m30 is her proven hit, dressed for weather. It's sensible, but there's no new idea, only good maintenance.

looks.comment: Reliable and genuinely pitch-ready. The m88 + m67 tonal leg with the midi hem overlapping the boot top is a correct, well-explained leg-lengthening move. At 9°C the m50 camel coat would be warmer and kinder near the face than the m51 black trench over silky jersey.

judgement.missedOpportunity: m45 check blazer over m01 leopard silk blouse tucked into m27 navy cigarette trousers, with m85 belt, m60 Chelsea boots, m80 hoops and m70 tan crossbody, under m50 camel coat. Leopard-on-check is the print mix she actually owns (her Friday blouse), the tan and rust warm her olive skin at the face, and the blazer finally reads as hers.
judgement.summary: A strong set with clear jobs: one look unlocks the unworn piece, one is joyful colour, one is the safe pitch option. Look 2 is excellent and Look 3 is dependable. Look 1 correctly reaches for m45 but plays it too muted for a colour-led client, so it needs a warm print or bright under the check before it goes out. Smaller practicality fixes: a work-sized bag in Look 2, a warmer coat in Look 3, and an honest note that black trenches sit at the face.

results.requestText: Dinner with friends at a nice restaurant on Saturday night.

looks.title: Baroque Romance, Rain-Ready
looks.idea: Her proven baroque wrap dress, kept sharp with flat knee-high boots and a red bag for a pop.
looks.howToWear: Tie the wrap snugly at the natural waist. Wear black opaque tights with the flat knee-high boots so the leg line runs unbroken from hem to boot. Stack the bangles on one wrist and wear the hoops with hair back. Carry the red mini bag on its short strap. Wear the trench belted over the top on the way there, then hang it up at the restaurant so the dress shows.
looks.why: This is the spirit of her gallery-opening look, which got compliments and felt like her: wrap dress, gold hoops, a warm-toned boot. The boots are waterproof enough for drizzle and flat for the Tube and walking. The tights and boots lengthen her shorter legs, and the red bag adds a warm bright without competing with the print. The black trench goes over the dress and comes off indoors, so it can't make the dress feel corporate.

looks.title: Emerald Velvet, Pink Tweed
looks.idea: Jewel-toned velvet made romantic and sharp with a cropped pink bouclé jacket.
looks.howToWear: Wear the velvet slip with black tights and the flat knee-high boots, so the bias hem skims the boot tops. Put the cropped tweed jacket on open or lightly buttoned. It stops at the waist, so it marks her waist and keeps the slip's line long. Add the pearl drops for a romantic edge and carry the beaded clutch. Put the camel coat over everything for the walk.
looks.why: Emerald is one of her best warm brights and works beautifully with her colouring. The velvet slip had only one outing. The pink and cream tweed is also barely worn and gives the sharp, polished element without a black blazer, which flattened her red dress. Cropped over a slip dress gives a defined waist, and the camel coat suits the colours and the 9°C weather.

looks.title: Check Blazer, Gold Satin
looks.idea: Tonal autumn colours and a mix of prints, with an oversized check blazer finally put to work.
looks.howToWear: Tuck the gold satin camisole into the navy cigarette trousers and cinch it with the wide black belt at the waist. Wear the oversized check blazer open over it with the sleeves pushed up to the forearm, so you see the belt and the drape of the satin. Wear the black Chelsea boots, hoops and bangles, and carry the tan crossbody. Put the camel coat over the top.
looks.why: The check blazer has never been worn because everything she tried it with got swamped. A slim, ankle-skimming trouser and a close-fitting camisole balance its volume, which avoids the top-and-bottom bulk that spoiled the tulle and jumper outfit. Rust, gold, navy and tan are warm and flatter her colouring. Gold satin brings in some romance and shine for the evening. The belt keeps her waist visible under a boyfriend cut, and the Chelsea boots handle drizzle.

output.note: I kept suede and calf-hair shoes out of tonight's looks because of the drizzle. The black Chelsea boots or flat knee-high boots are your best wet-weather options. Your wardrobe has no dressy flat that's both waterproof and colourful. If it stays dry on the night, the tan suede block-heel boots would work with the baroque dress or the check blazer look.

failures.detail: A near re-run of her proven gallery look (m30 + m80). It is reliable but adds no new idea. The 'sharp element' is only a red bag (m74).

The note cites 'a warm-toned boot' as the spirit of the original, then swaps tan suede for black m67. It also says tights and boots 'lengthen her legs' without noting that the black leg only reads long if the hem meets the boot top.

looks.comment: Practical and flattering: the wrap marks the waist, and m67/m88 cope with drizzle and walking. The black trench m51 is at the warm-weather end of acceptable at 9°C over silky jersey; the camel m50 would be warmer. Sendable, but it is the safe pick, not the inspired one.

failures.detail: It claims the boxy cropped m42 'marks her waist'. A boxy crop over a bias slip with no waist seam only ends at the waist; it doesn't define it. Leaving it open so the slip's line shows beneath is what actually reads hourglass, and the note should say so.

looks.comment: The strongest look: emerald velvet m38 with pink-cream bouclé m42 is a joyful, Michele-toned colour clash, and it revives two barely-worn pieces. The beaded clutch m73 adds an eclectic hit. Pearls m81 lean slightly ladylike; hoops m80 would give more edge, but this is a real point of view.

failures.detail: Billed as 'a mix of prints', but the check m45 is the only print in the look. The print-mixing promise in the idea isn't delivered.
A hip-length oversized boyfriend blazer cuts her at the widest point, which shortens legs that are already short relative to her torso. Under the long camel m50 it also stacks bulk at the shoulders.
The black belt m85 and black Chelsea boots m60 drop cold black accents into a brown/rust/navy/gold palette, while the bag m70 is tan. The neutrals muddle rather than echo.
Camel coat, brown check, navy trouser and tan bag read muted, close to the tasteful-neutral territory she avoids. There is little joy or colour beyond a sliver of gold satin.

looks.comment: Putting the orphaned m45 to work is the right instinct, but here it becomes a sober, office-ish outfit for a Saturday dinner. It needed a second print and a bright, not a cami and black hardware.

judgement.missedOpportunity: A three-scale print mix that properly launches the check blazer. Tuck the leopard silk blouse m01 into the black floral bias slip skirt m25, belted at the waist with m85, then put the oversized check blazer m45 on top, open. Finish with black tights m88, flat knee-high boots m67, hoops m80, the red mini bag m74 and the trench m51 for the walk. The prints run large check, medium leopard, small floral. Black and rust thread through all three, and the slim bias skirt balances the blazer's volume. This is Susie Bubble/Dries print-mixing that is still rain-safe.
judgement.summary: A solid set with good weather discipline, flat shoes throughout, and smart revival of the under-worn m38, m42 and m45. The honest note about suede in drizzle is welcome. Look 2 is the standout. Look 1 is a dependable but safe repeat of a proven formula. Look 3 needs reworking: it promises print-mixing it doesn't deliver, muddles black with brown neutrals, and drifts toward muted sobriety. Across all three, her core Style DNA of intentional print-mixing is barely used. Each look has at most one print.

results.requestText: Surprise me — put together something I wouldn't normally think of.

looks.title: Check Blazer, Finally
looks.idea: The never-worn check blazer over navy florals and cobalt: a print-mixed, colour-on-colour take on smart-casual.
looks.howToWear: Tuck the cobalt merino into the high-rise floral trousers and cinch the wide black belt over the jumper, so the waist shows under the oversized blazer. Wear the blazer open with the sleeves pushed up slightly to the forearm. Knot the rust silk scarf loosely at the neck, or tie it to the bag strap, to pick up the rust in the check. Chelsea boots under the full-length hems keep her dry. Camel coat on top for the walk.
looks.why: The navy floral and cobalt combination has already worked for her. The rust and brown check is the unexpected layer, and cobalt against rust is a flattering warm contrast. The belt keeps the oversized blazer from hiding her waist. It reads polished enough for a pitch, but it is print-mixed rather than corporate, and it finally gives the check blazer a job.

looks.title: Velvet by Day
looks.idea: An emerald velvet slip dress worn as a layered daytime piece: romantic, with a sharp cropped jacket.
looks.howToWear: Wear the ivory silk shirt under the slip dress with the collar out and the sleeves showing, buttoned at the cuff. Put the cropped pink tweed jacket on top, where its hem hits her natural waist. Add black opaque tights and the flat knee-high boots. Wear pearl drops and carry the red mini bag. Trench belted over everything in the drizzle.
looks.why: Layering the shirt under the slip gives full arm coverage and turns an evening dress into something for the office or an opening. Emerald and pink are warm, joyful colours near her face. The cropped jacket and bias-cut dress mark her waist and avoid the corporate black-blazer trap. The red bag adds one sharp, playful note.

looks.title: Mustard, Leopard, Burgundy
looks.idea: A warm-toned eclectic mix in which the leopard blouse sits against a pleated mustard skirt and a belted burgundy cardigan.
looks.howToWear: Tuck the leopard blouse into the high-waisted mustard skirt. Wear the burgundy longline cardigan open and belt it with the wide black belt at the waist for a defined middle and a long vertical line. Add black opaque tights and Chelsea boots, then hoops, the beret tilted back off the face, and the tan crossbody. Navy puffer on top for the cold and rain.
looks.why: This is her go-to leopard blouse in a new colour story. Mustard, burgundy and tan are all warm shades that flatter her colouring. The belted cardigan stops the pleats and longline layers from swamping her, which was the problem with the tulle and cable-knit outfit. The beret adds a romantic touch, and the puffer stays practical without being the focus.

output.note: I avoided the suede boots and calf-hair loafers because of the drizzle, and left out the mint blouse and powder blue skirt because they drain her colouring. The wardrobe has no real gaps for this brief.

failures.detail: The oversized boyfriend m45 under the straight below-knee m50 camel coat creates two bulky shoulder layers on a 164cm frame. The blazer sleeves will also bunch inside the coat. The long coat over full-length wide legs also cuts her short leg line.
In drizzle, m50 is the least rain-ready coat she owns. The water-resistant m51 trench would protect the never-worn wool check blazer better.

The scarf is 'at the neck, or tied to the bag strap'. That gives no decision. Floral at the neck on top of floral trousers and a large check is a third print, and the effect is very different from a scarf on the bag.

looks.comment: Giving m45 its first outing over the proven m20 + m10 colour-on-colour pairing is smart: the floral trousers and cobalt worked for her before, and the m45 check is the new element. The belt-under-open-blazer move keeps her waist. The outer layer is the wrong call for the weather and her proportions, and the stylist should commit to the scarf on the bag so the print count stays at two.

failures.detail: Three things crowd the neckline: the ivory shirt collar under the slip straps, the boxy boucle m42, and a belted trench m51 over the boucle. The boucle will fight the trench sleeves and shoulders.
Belted and closed in drizzle, the black trench m51 puts stark black at her face. That is exactly what drains her colouring, and it hides the pink and emerald story the look is built on.
It says the bias-cut slip 'marks her waist'. A bias slip skims rather than defines. Only the cropped jacket hem does that work.

looks.comment: This is the truest 'surprise me' of the three. Putting m38 velvet over the m13 shirt solves her arms-covered directive, and the m42 pink tweed with emerald and the m74 red bag is a joyful, Ganni-ish colour clash. The black tights into m67 knee boots also make a continuous leg line that helps her short legs. She should wear the trench open, or carry it, so the colour shows near her face.

failures.detail: A pleated midi m21, a belted longline cardigan m41 and a mid-length puffer m53 stack three volumes. The puffer will sit at or near the cardigan hem and erase the belted waist, which repeats the swamped feeling she disliked. Ankle-height Chelsea boots m60 under a midi also shorten her legs when the m67 knee-highs are available.
The m01 leopard blouse is her most-worn go-to, paired with her usual m60, m70 and m80. This is the least surprising look in a 'surprise me' brief.
The finishing layer is the m53 puffer, which she has said looks dull. That is a bad ending for a joyful, colour-forward look. The m51 trench was available and would keep the waist.

looks.comment: The mustard, leopard and burgundy palette is warm and flattering, and the beret is a nice romantic note. But this is her Friday blouse in a new skirt, and it is finished with the coat she dislikes over too many volumes. It needs the m67 knee boots and the m51 trench belted over everything before it goes out.

judgement.missedOpportunity: A true surprise that rescues two neglected pieces: m12 pink/orange abstract shirt worn over m10 cobalt merino (sleeves covered, camp collar out) tucked into m26 camel cord flares, with m45 check blazer, m83 resin flower earrings, m60 Chelsea boots, m74 red bag and m51 trench — print-on-print with warm brights at the face and a clear surprise factor.
judgement.summary: This is a good, thoughtful set. Look 1 finally gives the never-worn m45 a job, and Look 2 (velvet slip over a shirt with pink tweed) is a genuinely fresh idea that respects her arms-covered directive. The weak points are outerwear and layering bulk. The camel coat over an oversized blazer, the black trench over boucle, and the dull puffer over a belted longline cardigan all undercut proportions she cares about. In two of them the outer layer is also wrong for drizzle or for her colouring. Look 3 is the safe filler in a brief that asked for surprise. Fix the outer layers and swap the Chelsea boots for the knee-highs in Look 3, and this is ready to send.

results.requestText: It's raining all day and I'll be walking a lot. What should I wear?

looks.title: Baroque in the Rain
looks.idea: Her gallery-opening dress, made weatherproof with flat knee-high boots and a belted trench.
looks.howToWear: Wear the wrap dress with black opaque tights and flat knee-high boots, so the midi hem skims the boot tops and no wet leg shows. Belt the trench at the natural waist over the wrap to keep her hourglass line. Turn the trench collar up against the breeze. Add the gold hoops and a few bangles pushed up the wrist. Wear the tan crossbody under the coat so her hands stay free for walking and an umbrella.
looks.why: It repeats what worked for her: the baroque wrap, a defined waist and gold hoops. The long sleeves cover her arms, and flat boots under a midi are dry and easy to walk in. The trench keeps it polished, and the burgundy, gold and navy print is warm and flattering. It avoids the black-blazer-over-colour problem because the print is the focus.

looks.title: Emerald and Navy, Cropped for Puddles
looks.idea: A crisp colour-on-colour pitch-ready look with a cinched waist and ankle-skimming trousers.
looks.howToWear: Tuck the puff-sleeve emerald blouse neatly into the navy cropped trousers and cinch with the wide black belt to mark the waist. The cropped hem sits above the ankle rain boots, so nothing drags in puddles. Wear the trench open or belted over the top. Add the gold hoops and carry the red mini bag as the sharp pop of colour.
looks.why: Emerald and navy is a rich, warm-leaning pairing in the spirit of her cobalt-and-navy joy look. The structured puff sleeves cover her arms and add the romantic edge with polish. Cropped trousers are the sensible rain choice because they keep hems dry, and the belted high waist suits her proportions. The trench repeats from look one because it is her only polished waterproof layer. If this is a pitch day, swap the rain boots for the Chelsea boots once you arrive.

looks.title: Mustard and Cobalt Puffer Day
looks.idea: A joyful colour-blocked walking outfit that makes the practical puffer feel intentional.
looks.howToWear: Tuck the fine cobalt merino into the high-waisted mustard pleated skirt so the waist stays marked. Wear black opaque tights and the ankle rain boots. Zip the navy puffer over the top. Knot the silk floral scarf at the neck so its rust, navy and cream tones show at the collar. Add the burgundy beret and gold hoops. Carry the tan crossbody under the puffer or across your body over it.
looks.why: Cobalt and mustard are both warm brights that flatter her. The fine merino keeps her from feeling swamped, which was the problem with the cream jumper and tulle skirt. The scarf adds a print and a romantic touch, and the beret lifts the puffer she finds dull. It is the warmest and most practical option for a long walk in steady rain at 8°C.

output.note: Her only genuinely waterproof, polished layer is the black trench, so it appears in two looks. The navy puffer is the second weather-proof option. I left out the suede boots, the patent flats and the full-length wide-leg trousers because their hems and finishes would be ruined in all-day rain.

failures.detail: Turning the black trench (m51) collar up puts stark black right at her face, which her colouring notes say drains her. Nothing warm, such as the m84 rust/navy silk scarf, is placed between the collar and her face.
This is essentially her proven gallery look (m30 + hoops) with rain-proof boots swapped in. It is sound, but it adds no new idea or print-mix.

looks.comment: The formula is correct for the weather: a long-sleeved midi wrap with 60-denier tights (m88) and flat knee-high boots (m67) means no wet leg shows. Belting the trench at the waist keeps her hourglass line. It needs m84 knotted at the neck or the burgundy beret m87, which echoes the burgundy in the print, to break up the head-to-shin black and warm her face; silky jersey under unlined gabardine is also on the cool side for a breezy 8°C.

failures.detail: A poplin blouse (m02, warmth 2), stretch-cotton trousers (m27, warmth 2) and an unlined trench add up to too little warmth for a full day of walking in breezy 8°C rain.
The cropped cigarette hem (m27) ends above black ankle rain boots (m69). That bare-ankle gap chops legs that are already short relative to her torso, the opposite of what her proportions need.

Structured puff sleeves (m02) will crush inside the trench sleeves. The exposed ankle will get wet and cold. The 'swap to Chelsea boots for a pitch' advice is unworkable because the red mini bag (m74) cannot carry a second pair of boots.
There is no print anywhere for a print-led client, and rubber rain boots undercut the 'pitch-ready' claim.
It calls cropped trousers 'the sensible rain choice' but ignores the cold, wet ankle gap and the leg-shortening effect.

looks.comment: Emerald with navy and a red bag is a nice colour instinct, but the look is underdressed for the temperature and proportionally wrong for her legs. The pitch logic falls apart in practice. I would not send it.

failures.detail: Once the mid-length navy puffer (m53) is zipped, the tucked waist disappears, and the A-line pleats of m21 flare out beneath a padded volume. That stacks bulk on a short-legged frame.
It claims the fine merino stops her feeling swamped, but the merino is hidden under the puffer. The volume issue it cites is really decided by the coat.

looks.comment: Of the three, this best answers 'raining all day, walking a lot'. Making the puffer she finds dull feel intentional with the burgundy beret (m87) and the rust floral scarf (m84) at the collar is a genuinely good, Susie-Bubble-ish move. Cobalt and mustard is a flattering warm-bright clash. Wearing the puffer open while indoors, or belting it, would rescue her waist.

judgement.missedOpportunity:
A print-mixed rain look that keeps the waist and covers the arms for an office day:
- m01 leopard silk blouse tucked into the m21 mustard pleated midi, with m10 cobalt merino over it and the collar pulled out
- m88 black opaque tights with m67 flat knee-high boots
- m51 trench belted at the waist
- m84 rust/navy floral silk scarf at the neck to warm the black collar, with the m87 burgundy beret
- m80 gold hoops and the m70 tan crossbody
This uses her signature print, keeps her legs covered and dry, and is polished enough for a pitch.
judgement.summary: The stylist understood the rain mechanics: midi plus tights plus boots, no suede or full-length hems, and protected leather. Look 1 is reliable but safe, and Look 3 cleverly rescues the dull puffer. Look 2 is a real miss: too cold, a cropped ankle gap that shortens her legs, crushed puff sleeves and an unworkable shoe-swap plan. Across the set, her signature leopard blouse (m01) is unused, there is almost no print-mixing despite her print-led DNA, and black is left at her face under a turned-up trench collar. The note also wrongly lumps the patent flats with things rain would ruin. Patent leather is water-resistant; the real reason to avoid flats is wet feet. Competent and mostly wearable, but not yet the joyful, sharp rain-day answer this wardrobe can produce.

results.requestText: First date — cocktails at a smart bar.

looks.title: Baroque Wrap, Date-Night Edit
looks.idea: Her proven baroque wrap, sharpened with kitten heels and a red pop so it reads romantic and confident.
looks.howToWear: Wrap the dress snugly so the tie sits at the narrowest point of your waist. Add sheer-feeling black tights and the 4cm slingbacks. Wear the gold hoops and the bangle stack on one wrist only. Carry the red mini bag as the single sharp accent. Wear the camel coat open so the wrap neckline and waist show, and belt it only for the walk.
looks.why: The baroque wrap is her most complimented outfit and it is warm, long-sleeved and flattering on an hourglass shape. Burgundy, gold and navy suit her warm colouring. The black stays low at the legs and feet, away from her face. The 4cm heel is well under her 7cm limit and fine for the Tube. Leather shoes are the safer choice in drizzle than suede.

looks.title: Emerald Velvet, Tweed Twist
looks.idea: Jewel-toned velvet with a pink tweed jacket: romantic, slightly unexpected, and still polished.
looks.howToWear: Wear the slip dress with the cropped tweed jacket left open. It stops at the waist and keeps your proportions defined. Add black opaque tights and the flat knee-high boots so the hem and boot top overlap and make one long line. Wear the pearl drops and leave your neck bare. Carry the beaded clutch. Put the belted trench over everything for the drizzle and take it off at the bar.
looks.why: Emerald is one of her best colours. Pink against green is a joyful, Dries-Van-Noten-style pairing, and the bias-cut velvet is sleek on her waist. The tweed adds the one sharp, textured element and covers her shoulders. This look uses two under-worn pieces, and it avoids the black-blazer-over-party-dress mistake. The water-resistant trench and flat boots suit a wet walk.

looks.title: Check Blazer, Gold Camisole
looks.idea: A sharp, slightly undone tailoring look in warm autumn tones, with satin underneath for date-night heat.
looks.howToWear: Tuck the gold camisole into the navy cropped trousers. Add the wide black belt at the waist, with the blazer left open so the belt shows. Push the blazer sleeves up to the forearm. Wear the red Mary Janes and carry the red mini bag so the red repeats. Add the gold hoops and the bangles. Wear the camel coat over the top for the walk.
looks.why: This finally gives the unworn oversized check blazer a partner. The slim, cropped trousers balance the blazer's volume, so she isn't swamped. The belt keeps her waist defined. Gold, navy, rust and red sit well with her warm colouring. The red patent flats worked before with navy and are wet-weather friendly. The look is eclectic and relaxed without being casual.

output.note: I left out the tan suede boots because of the drizzle, and I kept the black blazer out of the mix so the looks stay colourful. Everything here is flat or under 5cm for the walk and Tube.

failures.detail: This is essentially her gallery-opening outfit (m30) with the suede boots swapped for m65. Wearing a proven dress to a first date is defensible, but the only new idea is the red bag (m74).

It says 'sheer-feeling black tights' when m88 is 60-denier opaque. That is a factual slip, and it changes the look, because opaque black plus black slingbacks makes the leg heavier and more office-like than sheer would.

looks.comment: A reliable, flattering, weather-appropriate answer: the long-sleeved wrap marks her waist, the warm baroque palette sits at her face, and the 4cm m65 handles the Tube. It is a proven formula rather than a new idea, and the red bag against burgundy is a tonal accent rather than a true 'sharp element'.

failures.detail: The boxy cropped m42 sits over a bias slip (m38) that does not cinch. Her waist is implied rather than marked. Flat knee-highs under a midi on a 164cm frame with short legs also give a slightly stumpy lower half. A 4cm heel or a visible waist point would help.

looks.comment: The strongest idea in the set. Emerald velvet against pink boucle is a genuine Dries-style colour clash in her best colours, and it finally gets m38 and m42 out of the cupboard. The water-resistant m51 and the flat boots make it honest for drizzle. Velvet, boucle and beading together (m73) are texture-heavy, but that suits her eclectic DNA, and the pearls (m81) keep it romantic.

failures.detail: An oversized hip-length boyfriend blazer (m45) over ankle-cropped slim trousers (m27) and flats cuts her already short leg twice: once at the hip, once at the ankle. It is the opposite of what her proportions need.

The wide black belt (m85) is the only black in a brown/rust/cream/gold/navy/red palette and reads as a stray. The red shoes and bag (m62, m74) also sit beside rust in the check without picking it up, so the red feels pasted on.
Cropped trousers with flats leave bare ankles at 9°C in drizzle, and she will be walking.
Only one print against plain navy, for a print-mixer. It reads as generic 'tailoring with a cami' rather than Maya, and leans pitch rather than romantic date.

looks.comment: Good instinct to activate the unworn m45 and the gold cami (m03), but the execution lets it down. Swap m27 for the high-rise, full-length navy floral m20 to get check-on-floral print-mixing, a longer leg and warm ankles. Drop m85 and let the red Mary Janes (m62) echo the floral's pink.

judgement.missedOpportunity: Look 3 done properly: m45 oversized check blazer over m03 gold satin cami tucked into m20 navy floral high-rise wide-leg trousers, with m62 red Mary Jane flats, m80 gold hoops, m82 bangles, m74 red mini bag and m50 camel coat. That gives check-on-floral print-mixing with intent, a long full-length leg line, covered ankles and gold at the face. Also unused: the m52 leopard faux-fur coat as statement outerwear over m38 would have been a very 'her' first-date entrance.
judgement.summary: A solid set with one excellent idea (Look 2's emerald and pink), one reliable banker (Look 1) and one under-resolved experiment (Look 3). The stylist read the weather well, avoiding suede and choosing m51 and leather shoes, respected the heel limit, and rightly avoided the black-blazer trap. Look 1 recycles a known win without adding much. Look 3 has proportion and colour-logic problems and misses the print-mixing that would make it hers. Fix Look 3 by swapping in m20 for m27 and removing the black belt, and correct the 'sheer tights' wording in Look 1, before sending.

results.requestText: Weekend brunch and then wandering around the shops.

looks.title: The Blazer Finally Gets Its Moment
looks.idea: A rust-and-cream check boyfriend blazer over cobalt and denim, with a silk scarf tying the colours together.
looks.howToWear: Wear the cobalt merino tucked into the high-rise jeans so your waist shows under the oversized blazer. Roll the blazer sleeves to the forearm and roll the jean hem once for a clean ankle. Knot the silk scarf loosely at the neck, with the rust showing against the cobalt. Tilt the burgundy beret back off your forehead for drizzle cover, and sling the tan crossbody across the body so it doesn't fight the blazer's volume.
looks.why: This puts the unworn blazer with the cobalt and jeans you already wear and love. Cobalt is one of your best colours and it sits at your face. The fitted tucked top under the roomy blazer avoids the swamped top-and-bottom volume that didn't work before. Brown and rust check against cobalt and a floral scarf is print-mixing with a bit of polish, and leather trainers are comfortable for hours of shopping.

looks.title: Mustard, Navy and a Little Romance
looks.idea: A pleated mustard midi with a Breton stripe, finished with a belted trench and a pop of red.
looks.howToWear: Tuck the Breton top fully into the high-waisted pleated skirt and let the trench hang open. Belt the trench if the drizzle picks up. Wear the black tights with the flat knee-high boots, so the skirt hem sits just above the boot tops. Tie the silk scarf at the bag strap or the neckline for the rust and navy. Wear the hoops and a few bangles, and carry the red mini bag on the shoulder.
looks.why: The mustard skirt marks your waist and the pleats move well when you walk. Mustard and navy stripes are warm and flattering, and they give you a joyful, slightly romantic look. The tights and the knee-high boots keep you warm and dry in 9° drizzle. The water-resistant trench gives the polish without a black blazer. The red bag is the one sharp element.

looks.title: Leopard Meets Floral
looks.idea: Two prints in a shared warm palette, with the waist belted and the camel coat wrapped over.
looks.howToWear: Tuck the leopard silk blouse into the high-rise floral wide-leg trousers, undo one more button than usual, and push the sleeves to three-quarter length. Add the wide black belt at the waist. The full-length trousers should skim the tops of the Chelsea boots. Wear the camel coat open over the top. Add the hoops and the stack of bangles, and wear the tan crossbody under the coat.
looks.why: This takes your Friday leopard blouse and pairs it with the floral trousers you've loved in colour-on-colour looks. The tan in the leopard picks up the camel coat, and the navy and pink floral stays calm against it. The belt and the high rise give your waist the definition you like, and the wide leg lengthens your legs. The wool coat and boots keep you warm and dry, and the look is easy to wear from brunch through the shops.

output.note: Everything here is leather or wool, so it holds up to light drizzle. I kept the suede block-heel boots and the calf-hair loafers out for that reason. You don't own an umbrella, so it may be worth taking one if the rain gets heavier.

failures.detail: No outerwear at 9°C in drizzle for hours outdoors. The m45 wool blazer over the m10 merino is the only real layer. It works for short hops but needs a plan for colder stretches, for example the m51 trench carried or worn over the top.

looks.comment: This is the best idea in the set. It activates the never-worn m45 check blazer by putting it with cobalt (m10), so the rust/brown against blue becomes a proper complementary clash. The m84 floral scarf adds a second print at a smaller scale, which is the correct way to mix against a large check. The tuck and the open blazer handle her waist, but she should know it is under-layered for a long drizzly day.

failures.detail: The m06 cotton Breton (warmth 2) is the only top layer under an unlined m51 trench worn open. That is cold at 9°C for hours of wandering. The m10 cobalt merino would have been warmer and bolder.
Breton + skirt + black trench + black boots is a stock 'Parisian weekend' formula. Black trench, tights and boots dominate the look, so it reads more classic than print-led or eclectic.
The black m51 trench collar frames her face. The scarf could break that up, but the stylist hedges with 'bag strap or neckline' instead of committing to the neck.
The m21 midi skirt hangs below the knee-length m51 trench, which gives a messy double hem line when the coat is closed or belted.
Nothing here is 'romantic', and a red bag (m74) is a colour pop, not the 'sharp element' her DNA describes. The rationale relabels pieces rather than explaining them.

looks.comment: This is competent but it is the weakest look. Mustard and navy stripe is pleasant, but the look leans on black and does not feel like Maya. Swap m06 for m10 cobalt merino and tie m84 at the neck, and it becomes a warm colour-block she would actually be excited by.

failures.detail: Full-length crepe m20 wide-leg trousers over flat m60 Chelsea boots will drag and wick up wet pavement during a day of walking in drizzle. Advise a slight cuff, or remind her to check the hem length with the boots on.

'Shared warm palette' is inaccurate: the m20 floral is navy/pink/green, which is cool-leaning. The mix actually works because leopard acts as a neutral and the black belt picks up the leopard's black. The 'wide leg lengthens your legs' claim only holds if the hem nearly covers the boot.

looks.comment: Leopard (m01) with floral (m20) is exactly her Susie Bubble DNA. The m50 camel coat is the right warm layer and echoes the tan in the leopard. It is close to her proven Friday look, so it is a reliable hit rather than a discovery, but the trouser hem in drizzle needs a practical note.

judgement.missedOpportunity: The m42 pink tweed jacket (cropped exactly at her waist, worn once) over the m10 cobalt merino, with the m24 high-rise jeans, m60 Chelsea boots, m74 red mini bag and m80 hoops, and the m50 camel coat over the top for warmth. It is pink-red-cobalt colour play in a Ganni key. It marks her waist without a belt and puts cobalt at her face, and it solves the drizzle question better than suede or crepe hems.
judgement.summary: This is a solid edit with one genuinely good move: finally styling the unworn m45 check blazer with cobalt and a floral scarf. Look 3 is reliably on-brand print-mixing, though full-length crepe hems in drizzle need a warning. Look 2 is the weak link: it is underdressed for 9°C, black-heavy, generic, and its explanation mislabels a red bag as the 'sharp element'. The weather thinking is uneven. Look 1 has no coat, and the stylist's note that 'everything here is leather or wool' only applies to the shoes. The under-used m42 pink tweed jacket and m02 emerald blouse were left on the rail. Before sending, fix Look 2 (swap in m10 and commit m84 to the neck) and add a coat note to Look 1.

results.requestText: I'm presenting to senior leadership next week. I want to look authoritative but still like me.

looks.title: The Check Blazer, Finally
looks.idea: Tonal blues under a warm oversized check blazer: authority from tailoring, personality from colour.
looks.howToWear: Tuck the cobalt merino into the cigarette trousers and cinch it with the wide black belt so the waist reads under the oversized blazer. Wear the blazer open with the sleeves pushed up just once, so the cuff sits at the wrist and the shoulders stay slouchy. The cropped hem and Chelsea boots keep the leg line clean. Stack the bangles on one wrist and wear the hoops. The camel coat goes over the top for the Tube.
looks.why: The slim cropped trouser balances the oversized blazer, so you avoid the swamped volume that didn't work before. Cobalt next to rust and brown check is a warm, flattering mix, and it gives you the boardroom look in your own colours. It also finally puts m45 to work and avoids the corporate-black-blazer trap. Arms are covered and the flat boots can handle the drizzle.

looks.title: Baroque Authority
looks.idea: Your proven gallery-opening dress, sharpened for the boardroom with sleek flat boots and a trench.
looks.howToWear: Wear the wrap dress with the wrap tied snugly at the natural waist and the hem just above the top of the flat knee-high boots, with sheer-looking black tights where the hem and boot meet. Keep jewellery to the hoops and a few bangles so the print stays the star. Wear the belted trench cinched over the top for the commute and take it off in the room. Carry the black tote for your laptop.
looks.why: It marks your waist and has long sleeves, and the burgundy, gold and navy baroque print is rich and warm against your skin. It is the dress that has already made you feel completely like yourself, and the dark knee-high boot gives it the polish of a power look without adding a blazer. The water-resistant trench handles the drizzle and the flat boots work for the walking.

looks.title: Emerald Command
looks.idea: Sharp black tailoring with a saturated emerald top: decisive, a bit romantic, unmistakably yours.
looks.howToWear: Tuck the crisp puff-sleeve blouse into the high-rise wide-leg trousers and add the wide belt over the blouse to define the waist. Let the trousers skim the floor over the kitten heels to lengthen your legs. Keep the gold hoops and bangles. Wear the camel coat on the commute, and put the heels on at the office if the pavements are slick.
looks.why: The black trousers are your most authoritative piece, and emerald is one of your flattering warm brights, so the black sits away from your face and doesn't drain you. The puff sleeves are the romantic edge and the sharp crease is the polish. The high rise and belt mark your waist, the 4cm heel keeps within your limit, and the arms are covered.

output.note: The black blazer is deliberately left out. For this pitch the check blazer, baroque dress and emerald blouse give polish with more personality. If you want a fourth option, the ivory silk shirt with the black trousers and pink tweed jacket would be a softer version.

failures.detail: m27 slim cropped trousers ending at black m60 Chelsea boots put a colour break at the ankle and shorten a leg line she has already flagged as short. m27's rise isn't stated, so the tuck-and-belt plan may not land at the natural waist.
For a print-led client, m45 is the only pattern and everything under it is solid. The check is treated as a neutral rather than as the start of a print conversation.

'Sleeves pushed up just once so the cuff sits at the wrist' is muddled. The note doesn't address fitting the straight m50 coat over an oversized boyfriend blazer, or the black belt sitting against navy, cobalt and brown.

looks.comment: Finally activating m45 with cobalt m10 is the right instinct, and rust-against-cobalt is a genuinely good colour call. But the solid navy/cobalt base makes it a tidy tailoring look rather than a Maya look. Swapping m27 for a high-rise wide-leg would also fix the leg line.

failures.detail: It asks for 'sheer-looking' tights where the hem meets the boot, but m88 is 60-denier opaque. With a midi hem and knee-high m67 there shouldn't be a gap to manage anyway.
This is essentially her proven gallery look with the boots swapped. It never really answers the aspiration to look more authoritative at pitches; the polish comes only from black accessories.

looks.comment: A reliable, flattering and weather-sound choice. m30's wrap, sleeves and warm print plus continuous dark m88/m67 legs is a good lengthening move. It is comfortable rather than elevated: nothing in it signals 'senior leadership' beyond what she'd wear to a gallery.

failures.detail: Solid emerald m02 over solid black m23 with black belt, heels and tote has no print at all. It reads as a generic 'colour top plus black trousers' office formula, not print-led eclecticism.

No commute shoe is named for drizzle and lots of walking; it only says to 'put the heels on at the office'. Floor-skimming m23, hemmed for a kitten heel, will drag wet if she commutes in flats. Structured puff sleeves will also crush under the straight m50 coat.

Boxy hip-length poplin with structured puffs, stuffed into full wide-leg trousers, edges toward the volume-top-and-bottom problem she reported with m22/m09. The belt helps, but a crisp boxy poplin tucks bulkily.
Sleeve length of m02 isn't confirmed, so the 'arms covered' claim is asserted rather than checked. Commute footwear is missing.

looks.comment: Polished and the emerald is well placed at the face. But it is the least 'her' of the three, solves authority by borrowing corporate black, and leaves the wet commute half-planned.

judgement.missedOpportunity: A controlled print-mix that delivers authority without losing her: m45 check blazer worn open over m01 leopard silk blouse tucked into m23 black high-rise wide-leg trousers. The two prints share a tan/brown/cream/black palette, so the clash has logic. The silk tuck marks her waist and the pressed wide leg lengthens her legs. Finish with m65 kitten slingbacks in the room and m60 Chelsea boots for the commute, m80 hoops and m82 bangles, m71 tote, and m51 trench for the drizzle. That is Dries-meets-boardroom.
judgement.summary: A competent, wearable set that sensibly sidelines the black blazer and finally gives m45 a job. It also respects her directives on heel height, sleeves and no strapless. The weakness is that a print-led, eclectic client gets one print per look at most, and none at all in Look 3, so 'still like me' is undersold. Look 1 is a good idea held back by a cropped slim trouser and solid-on-solid layers. Look 2 is safe and flattering but a repeat rather than an upgrade. Look 3 is a generic office formula with an unresolved wet commute. Push the check blazer into an actual print-mix with m01 and high-rise m23, and this becomes the answer she's been looking for.

results.requestText: Wedding guest — outdoor afternoon ceremony, and the forecast says it might rain.

looks.title: Baroque and Belt
looks.idea: Your most proven romantic print, made rain-proof with flat knee boots and a belted trench.
looks.howToWear: Wear the wrap dress with the waist tie pulled snug so the defined waist is the focus. Add black opaque tights under flat knee-high boots, which are steady on wet grass. Belt the trench over the dress at the same height as the wrap, cinching it so the waist reads twice. Keep the tan crossbody across the body for hands-free umbrella duty. Chunky hoops are the only jewellery needed, since the print carries the look.
looks.why: This is the spirit of your gallery-opening dress, which got the compliments. It has long sleeves, a defined waist and a midi length that suits your proportions. The flat boots and water-resistant trench handle drizzle and a lawn. The burgundy, gold and navy print is rich and warm against your colouring, and nothing black sits at your face.

looks.title: Velvet and Tweed
looks.idea: Emerald velvet with a pink tweed jacket: joyful, romantic, one sharp waist-cropped edge.
looks.howToWear: Put the velvet slip on with the cropped tweed jacket buttoned or just closed at the waist, so the jacket's hem sits at your narrowest point and the bias skirt falls from there. The jacket covers your arms and stops the slip from feeling bare in November. Add black tights and flat Chelsea boots, with the hem skimming the boot tops. Wear small pearl drops and carry the beaded clutch. Put the camel coat over the top for the walk in and take it off for photos.
looks.why: Emerald is one of your strongest colours and pink gives it a warm, romantic lift. The tweed jacket is under-worn and finishes the dress with a sharp, polished element, without the corporate feel of the black blazer. Flat boots keep you safe on damp ground. The beaded clutch brings in multicolour to link the pink and green.

looks.title: Mustard, Emerald, Red
looks.idea: Warm brights stacked on purpose: crisp emerald sleeves over a pleated mustard midi, with a red pop.
looks.howToWear: Tuck the boxy poplin blouse fully into the high-waisted pleated skirt so the waist is clean and defined, and let the puff sleeves be the statement. Wear black opaque tights with the red patent Mary Janes. Patent wipes clean and flats are good on grass. Add hoops and a couple of bangles, and carry the red mini bag so it matches your shoes. Wear the camel coat open over the top, which keeps the look warm-toned.
looks.why: This is colour-on-colour in the way that felt joyful before, and every piece is a warm bright that flatters you. The puff sleeves cover your arms, and the high-rise pleated skirt balances your short legs and torso. Two under-worn pieces (the blouse and the skirt) get used, and the red accents add personality while the look stays polished enough for a wedding.

output.note: Your wardrobe has no umbrella, so bring one. I kept the tan suede boots and the leopard faux-fur coat out of the forecast drizzle. I also avoided the mint blouse, which drains you, and the powder blue tulle skirt, which has already overwhelmed you. Mid-blue jeans and the cobalt jumper are too casual for a ceremony. Two coats cover three looks, so the camel coat appears twice.

failures.detail: m30 is a near-copy of the proven gallery look. The only changes are rain logistics: black m67 boots, black m88 tights and the black m51 trench. Nothing in it is new or specific to a wedding.
Her known miss is a black blazer making a red dress feel corporate. Here, black trench, tights and knee boots box in the burgundy/gold print in the same way.
Once the m51 trench is on, its black collar sits right at her face. That contradicts the stylist's claim that nothing black is near it. A warm scarf (m84) at the neck would have fixed this.
'The waist reads twice' is the only real technique given. There is no wedding-specific lift, and hoops plus a tan everyday crossbody (m70) read like a gallery night, not a ceremony.

looks.comment: This is practical and flattering: a long-sleeve wrap midi, flat boots for wet grass and a water-resistant trench. But it is the gallery dress in rain gear, with a lot of black and no wedding polish. Add m84 knotted at the neck, m82 bangles and the m74 red bag, and it becomes a look rather than a solution.

failures.detail: Silk-style velvet (m38) marks and crushes in drizzle. The m50 camel wool coat is not water-resistant, so the most fragile fabric has the least rain protection. The water-resistant m51 trench should have gone here instead.

Everyday m60 Chelsea boots (formality 2, worn 25x) under a velvet slip, with pearls and the m73 beaded clutch, pull the look back down to a weekday. The m62 red patent Mary Janes are wipe-clean, flat and would complete the joy.
A boxy, waist-cropped boucle jacket (m42) closed over a bias slip can square off her hourglass. It needs to be worn open, or the 'narrowest point' claim needs a defined-waist mechanism to back it up.
There is no print at all in a client whose DNA is print-led. The look is colour-forward, but m84 or a leopard note would make it unmistakably hers.

looks.comment: Emerald velvet with pink tweed is the strongest idea in the set: Gucci-toned-down romance with a sharp crop, and it puts two neglected pieces to work. It is let down by the rain-unsafe coat choice and the casual Chelsea boots.

failures.detail: Structured puff sleeves on a boxy blouse (m02) plus a pleated A-line midi (m21) put volume top and bottom. That is exactly the 'swamped' complaint from the tulle and cable-knit look, and the stylist calls it balancing.
Cotton poplin and crepe at 9°C for an outdoor ceremony, with the m50 coat 'worn open' in drizzle. Thin flats (m62) with tights on a wet lawn also mean wet feet.
A crisp poplin blouse with a skirt reads as a creative office day, not a wedding. Formality-3 separates are the weakest register option among her dresses.
Black opaque tights between a mustard midi and red shoes break the leg line on short legs. The matched red shoes and bag (m62/m74) feel dated rather than intentional.
The claim that the high-rise pleated skirt 'balances your short legs and torso' is not argued. The volume issue is ignored.

looks.comment: The colour stack is genuinely joyful and well chosen for her colouring. But the silhouette repeats her documented volume miss, and the outfit is too cold and too office-casual for an outdoor November wedding.

judgement.missedOpportunity: Print-mixing for a print-led client, with the never-worn m45 oversized check blazer finally given a home. The m30 baroque wrap dress with m45 worn open and sleeves pushed: the rust/brown/cream check and the burgundy/gold baroque share a warm palette, so the clash reads as Dries rather than chaos, and the open blazer keeps the wrap waist visible. Add m88 tights, m67 flat knee boots, m80 hoops, m82 bangles and the m74 red bag, with the m51 trench over the top for rain and m84 knotted at the neck to keep black off her face. Alternatively, fix Look 2 by putting m51 over m38/m42 and swapping m60 for m62.
judgement.summary: A sensible, weather-aware set that respects her directives: flats or low heels, covered arms, no strapless, and a sensible note about the suede boots and the faux-fur coat. Look 1 is a safe repeat drowned in black. Look 2 has the best idea but puts velvet under a non-waterproof coat and in casual boots. Look 3 repeats her volume miss and is too cold and too office for a wedding. Most strikingly, a print-mixing client gets one print across three looks, and the unworn check blazer, the obvious eclectic sharp element, is ignored.

results.requestText: How should I wear my oversized check blazer (m45)?

looks.title: Colour-on-Colour with a Check Twist
looks.idea: Your joyful cobalt-and-navy-floral combination, with the check blazer as the sharp, grown-up layer.
looks.howToWear: Tuck the cobalt merino into the high-rise floral trousers so the waist shows, and let the hems skim the tops of the Mary Janes. Wear the blazer open with the sleeves pushed up once, to show the wrist and keep the shape from swamping you. Keep the jewellery to the gold hoops. Wear the black trench over everything for the drizzle and carry the tan crossbody.
looks.why: This is the formula that already worked for you: colour-on-colour with red patent flats. The rust in the check picks up the pink in the floral, and the cobalt cuts through the warm browns. The blazer adds polish for the office without the corporate feel of your black one. High-rise trousers and a tucked-in knit keep the oversized blazer from hiding your waist.

looks.title: Pitch-Day Pleats
looks.idea: Warm, autumnal tailoring where a silk scarf ties the check and the mustard together.
looks.howToWear: Tuck the ivory silk shirt into the mustard pleated skirt. Knot the rust, navy and cream scarf loosely at the collar, with the shirt's top button open. Put the blazer on and belt it at the natural waist with the wide black belt, so the oversized shape gets an hourglass. Add black opaque tights and the flat knee-high boots, which also cope with the wet pavements. Put the camel coat over the top for the commute.
looks.why: Belting the blazer marks your waist and turns a boyfriend cut into something deliberate and polished, which suits a client pitch. Mustard, rust and ivory are warm and flattering on you, and the scarf repeats the check's colours so the print mix looks planned. Your arms are covered, there are no heels, and it stays colourful and a little romantic with the pleats and silk.

looks.title: Velvet and Check After Dark
looks.idea: A romantic emerald slip with a slouchy check blazer thrown over it, for dinner or a gallery opening.
looks.howToWear: Wear the emerald velvet slip as the base and drape the blazer over it, either open or with the shoulders slightly slipped off. Roll the sleeves to the forearm so the bangles show. Add black opaque tights and the Chelsea boots to take the sweetness down a notch. Carry the red mini bag for a tomato pop against the emerald. Add the gold hoops and bangle stack, and wear the trench belted over the top for the walk and the drizzle.
looks.why: Emerald is one of your best colours, and the rust-brown check sits well with it. The slip gives the romantic element and the oversized blazer gives the sharp one, which is your Style DNA. The blazer also covers your arms, since the slip has thin straps. Flat boots keep it comfortable on the Tube and in the rain, and the red bag finishes it without the black-blazer-over-red problem, because this blazer is warm rather than corporate.

output.note: Every look uses the check blazer (m45), as you asked, with a different anchor piece in each so you get three different ways to wear it. Avoid the tan suede boots in this drizzle, and the Breton top or leopard blouse with jeans would also work under it for a weekend. The blazer pairs best with solid or small-scale pieces in warm brights, and it has no formal black to fall back on, which is the point.

failures.detail: 'The rust in the check picks up the pink in the floral' isn't true: rust and pink are different temperatures. The real link is the navy-floral/cobalt cool block against the warm brown check, plus the scale contrast between a large check and a medium floral. That is the lesson she needed.

The full-length crepe wide-legs (m20) are told to 'skim the tops' of thin patent flats (m62) for a day of walking in drizzle. The hems will wick water. A rolled hem or a half-inch cuff should have been specified.

A hip-length boyfriend blazer over full wide-legs on a 164cm frame with short legs is a lot of width top and bottom. The tuck only works if the blazer stays open, and the stylist half-says this but should state it outright.

looks.comment: A smart, low-risk entry point: m45 is grafted onto her proven m10/m20/m62 colour-on-colour formula, and the large check against a medium floral is a legitimate scale mix. It needs a hem fix for the wet and a more honest colour rationale.

failures.detail: Belting an oversized wool boyfriend blazer (m45) at the waist creates a stiff peplum flare. That flare then sits directly on a pleated A-line midi (m21): bulk over volume, cutting a short-legged 164cm frame at mid-hip.
She already felt swamped by 'too much volume top and bottom' (m22 + m09). An oversized blazer belted over pleats is the same structural mistake in tailoring form.
Camel coat (m50), brown check, mustard, ivory and rust read as a tonal autumn heritage look. It is closer to the warm-neutral polish she says would betray her than to colour-forward Dries.

The wide black belt (m85), black tights (m88) and black boots (m67) drop a cold black into an all-warm palette with no other black to answer them. The belt in particular becomes a hard horizontal stripe at the waist.

looks.comment: The instinct is right: a pitch look, the m84 scarf echoing the check, and arms covered. But the execution would swamp her. Keep the scarf and the shirt, and swap the pleated skirt for a slim bottom such as the navy cigarette trousers (m27) so the oversized blazer has a narrow base.

failures.detail: 'Shoulders slightly slipped off' is an editorial-shoot gesture. It is not a styling move for a real gallery opening in November, and it would leave her adjusting the blazer all night.

looks.comment: This is the best look. It activates the barely-worn emerald velvet (m38) and pairs complementary emerald with rust-brown check, with velvet against wool for texture. It hits her romantic-plus-one-sharp-element DNA exactly. The explanation cleverly cites why this warm blazer avoids her black-blazer-over-red failure, though the red bag (m74) against emerald edges toward festive, so keep the rest gold.

judgement.missedOpportunity: Leopard-and-check, the defining Michele/Susie Bubble print clash this blazer was made for, used as the pitch look. Tuck the leopard silk blouse (m01) into the navy cropped cigarette trousers (m27) and put the check blazer (m45) on open with the sleeves pushed up. Add black Chelsea boots (m60) for the drizzle, gold hoops (m80), the tan crossbody (m70) and the black trench (m51). The slim cropped trouser balances the oversized blazer on her short legs, and the fluid leopard against crisp large-scale check is the polished-but-unmistakably-her answer to her aspiration. The stylist mentions leopard in the note but never builds the look.
judgement.summary: A good set with a clear job for each look: office colour-on-colour, pitch, and evening. Every look uses m45 as asked, and the weather handling is sensible, with suede boots ruled out and trench or camel coat over each look. Look 3 is genuinely excellent and Look 1 is a solid extension of a proven formula. Look 2 is the weak link: belting an oversized blazer over a pleated midi rebuilds her known 'volume top and bottom' miss, and the all-warm-neutral palette with stray black accents drifts away from her colour-forward DNA. That matters because Look 2 is the pitch look, the one tied to her stated aspiration. The colour rationale is sometimes hand-wavy. Fix Look 2 with a slim bottom (m27), or replace it with leopard-and-check, before sending.

results.requestText: Long travel day tomorrow — I want to be comfortable but still look put-together.

looks.title: Camel & Cobalt Traveller
looks.idea: Colour-on-colour warmth with a printed silk scarf as the one sharp, romantic touch.
looks.howToWear: Tuck the cobalt merino into the high-rise corduroy flares so the waist stays marked and the flare lengthens your leg line. Wear the flares over the Chelsea boots so only the toe shows. Knot the rust, navy and cream silk scarf loosely at the neck, with the tails tucked into the jumper. Belt the trench at the waist and wear the crossbody across your body so your hands are free. Add the gold hoops.
looks.why: Cobalt and camel are the same warm-neutral and warm-bright pairing she loves, and it echoes her navy and cobalt colour-on-colour look. Everything is soft and stretchy enough for hours of sitting. Corduroy and merino are warm on a cold plane, and the Chelsea boots and water-resistant trench cope with drizzle. The scarf keeps it from reading as a plain travel uniform.

looks.title: Print-on-Print Easy Layers
looks.idea: Stripe meets floral in a shared navy, softened with burgundy and finished with a camel coat.
looks.howToWear: Tuck the Breton top into the high-rise navy floral wide-legs so the waist is clear and the trousers skim the white trainers. Layer the burgundy longline cardigan open over the top, so it adds a vertical line and sits easily on a plane. Wear the camel coat open over the top and carry the tote. Add the hoops and the gold bangle stack.
looks.why: The navy runs through both prints, so the mix looks intentional rather than busy. The burgundy picks up the colour in the floral. It's the most comfortable look of the three: crepe trousers, cotton jersey and trainers made for walking. The layers come off easily when the Tube or the terminal is warm, and the camel coat makes it look polished rather than sporty.

looks.title: Baroque Wrap, Travel-Ready
looks.idea: Her most flattering print dress, made practical with tights, flat boots and a beret.
looks.howToWear: Wear the baroque wrap dress with the black opaque tights and flat knee-high boots, so the line from hem to boot is continuous. Tie the wrap snugly at the waist. Set the burgundy beret slightly back on the head and add the hoops and bangles. Wear the navy puffer open or zipped over the top, and carry the tote.
looks.why: The wrap dress is a proven winner for her. It marks the waist, has long sleeves and stretches in silky jersey, so it's as comfy as a loungewear piece. Tights and tall flat boots keep her warm and dry. The beret picks up the burgundy in the print, and the navy puffer echoes the navy in the dress, so the practical coat looks chosen. The one compromise is that the puffer is her least favourite piece, but it's the best choice for a wet, cold travel day.

output.note: I left out the black blazer, mint blouse and powder-blue skirt. They don't suit her colouring or the day, and the blazer is her usual default. The oversized check blazer would be bulky over everything else for a long journey, so it's better saved for an office day. Pack a spare layer, such as the burgundy cardigan, in your tote because planes and trains can be cold.

failures.detail: For a print-led, eclectic client, the only pattern is the m84 scarf. That is the most restrained reading of her Style DNA. The m01 leopard blouse (her proven Friday look) could have been tucked into m26 for the same comfort with more of her.

The claim that everything is 'soft and stretchy' is not reliably true of corduroy. The link to the navy and cobalt look is loose: that look worked because of the print against the bright, not cobalt against a neutral.

looks.comment: A sound, weather-proof travel look. The m51 water-resistant trench, the slip-on m60 Chelsea boots for security and the hands-free m70 crossbody are all smart. The cobalt and camel pairing flatters her warm colouring, and the m84 scarf keeps the black trench collar off her face. It is competent and polished, but it is the least 'Maya' version of this outfit.

failures.detail: Full-length crepe wide-legs (m20) over flat white trainers (m63) will drag hems through drizzle and puddles all day. The m50 wool coat is the only outer layer that is not water-resistant, on a wet day.

The m41 longline cardigan sits open under the m50 below-the-knee coat, over full-length wide-legs. That stacks two long layers on a 164cm frame with short legs. It buries the waist the tuck was meant to mark and makes her look swamped.
'The burgundy picks up the colour in the floral' is false: m20 is navy/pink/green, with no burgundy. The burgundy is a fourth colour story, not a link.
The m82 bangle stack is a nuisance at airport security on a travel day.

looks.comment: The stripe-on-floral idea, linked by navy, is the most on-brand concept in the set. But the execution fights both the weather and her proportions. Swap m06+m41 for her proven m10 cobalt merino, m63 for m60 Chelsea boots, and m50 for m51 and it becomes the best look of the three.

failures.detail: The mid-length m53 puffer over a midi wrap dress hides the defined waist that is the whole reason m30 works. The silhouette becomes a column of nylon over a hem.

She explicitly finds m53 dull, and the water-resistant, belted m51 trench is available. Belted over m30, it would keep the waist and the polish and still handle the drizzle. Choosing the puffer is defaulting to practicality when a better practical option exists.
There is no note on securing the wrap (a hidden pin or snap) for hours of sitting, when wrap fronts shift. The m82 bangles will be a hassle at security again.

looks.comment: A smart use of her proven m30, with m88 tights and m67 knee boots giving a continuous line that helps her leg length. The m87 beret picking up the burgundy is a genuinely nice, rain-useful touch. The coat choice undercuts it: the stylist even flags the puffer as her least favourite and uses it anyway.

judgement.missedOpportunity: m01 leopard silk blouse tucked into m26 camel corduroy flares, with the unworn m45 oversized brown/rust/cream check blazer as the cabin layer. Leopard and check share tan and rust, so it is a print mix with intent. Add m60 Chelsea boots, m51 belted trench for the drizzle, m71 tote, m80 hoops and the m84 scarf in the bag. This is comfortable, warm and polished, gets the never-worn blazer into rotation, and feels far more like her than cobalt and camel. A boyfriend blazer is a classic travel layer, not a bulky one.
judgement.summary: Look 1 is the only look I'd send as-is: practical, flattering and polished, but light on her print-led personality. Look 2 has the right instinct but fails on drizzle, proportion and a false colour claim. Look 3 smartly reuses her proven wrap dress, but the disliked puffer swallows the waist when the water-resistant trench was right there. The note dismissing m45 as bulky misses its value as a travel layer, and the bangles on a security-heavy day show nobody walked through the actual journey. It's a competent set, but it needs a revision pass before it goes to Maya.

results.requestText: What should I wear to work tomorrow?

looks.title: Earth and Green
looks.idea: Warm, tonal texture in forest green and chocolate, which is the colour he's been missing, and still quiet.
looks.howToWear: Wear the forest green merino with its hem left out over the chocolate cords, with the sleeves pushed to mid-forearm. Cuff the cords once, just above the lug boots, so the boot shape shows and the hem stays clear of the chain. Put the olive waxed jacket over the top with the corduroy collar up for the wind, and tuck the navy scarf inside it. Brown belt, steel watch, and the roll-top backpack for the ride.
looks.why: The cords have only been worn twice because he wasn't sure what to wear them with. Forest green is in his palette and sits well against his cool colouring, and brown sits underneath it. The relaxed wide-wale cords are easy to pedal in, and the waxed jacket and rainproof lug boots handle the showers and wind. It is textural, warm and understated, with no navy-and-grey default.

looks.title: Soft Tailoring, Tonal Grey
looks.idea: His winter presentation formula, adapted to be rideable: the roll-neck and flannel, with a blazer in place of the overcoat.
looks.howToWear: Wear the charcoal roll-neck tucked loosely at the front only, so the flannel trousers keep a clean straight line. Layer the unlined navy blazer over it with the sleeves left at full length, which suits his long arms. Add the black belt to match the Chelsea boots. For the ride, wear the black rain shell over everything and take it off at the studio. The blazer stays dry and uncrushed underneath.
looks.why: This repeats the look that felt sharp at his last winter presentation, but swaps the knee-length overcoat for a blazer and a hip-length shell, which keeps it rideable. The lambswool, flannel and soft-shouldered blazer give plenty of texture. The Chelsea boots have a rubber sole for grip. It also works if a client drops in or a jacket is needed, and no tie is required.

looks.title: Rust Cord, Quietly
looks.idea: A muted rust corduroy shirt set against ecru and navy, so the colour reads as warmth rather than a statement.
looks.howToWear: Wear the rust cord shirt open at the collar over the ecru tee, so the ecru sits against his face and the rust stays further down. Leave the shirt untucked and roll the sleeves twice to the forearm. Tuck the tee into the navy pleated trousers under it. Wear the charcoal quilted liner under the black rain shell for the ride. Drape the navy scarf at the neck, which also keeps the rust off his face. Brown belt and steel watch.
looks.why: The rust shirt has only been worn twice, and here it adds the warmth he wants without sitting close to his face, where strong orange tones don't suit him. The navy pleated trousers are his dependable base and the brown derbies are his proven studio shoe, so it feels like his own style with one change. The liner and shell give wind and rain protection. The crepe-soled derbies are fine for a short ride, but suede can mark in a downpour, so swap to the lug boots if it is raining hard when you leave.

output.note: I've assumed a studio day with no client presentation, and that you are cycling. If you do have a presentation, Look 2 is the one to wear. I left out the camel suede trucker because of the showers, and the penny loafers because they are slippery on wet pedals.

looks.comment: The best look here. It finally gives the twice-worn chocolate cords (d26) a job, using forest green merino (d12) in his cool palette and the navy scarf (d62) to keep cool colour at the face, and it is fully rideable with the waxed jacket (d41) and lug boots (d55). Pushing the d12 sleeves is the right fix for his long arms. Two small notes: olive over forest green can read muddy, so the navy scarf matters, and the grey cashmere beanie (d63) belongs on a windy 6°C ride.

failures.detail: Navy blazer (d30), charcoal roll-neck (d05), grey flannel (d21) and black boots (d51) is exactly the navy-and-grey loop he asked to break. Nothing in it answers his aspiration for more warmth.

An unlined soft-shoulder blazer under a hip-length shell, with backpack straps on top for 25 minutes, will arrive creased at the shoulders. It will not stay 'uncrushed'. The flannel legs are also exposed to the showers.

'Sleeves left at full length, which suits his long arms' is meaningless, since standard sleeves are his problem, not his solution. The front-only tuck of a roll-neck under a blazer works against the precise, clean line he wants and is not explained.

looks.comment: A sensible presentation fallback, but as a third option it is a recycled formula with filler reasoning. Warming it up would have answered the brief and the aspiration at once: swap in d12 forest green or d55 brown boots with the brown belt (d65), and put the waxed jacket (d41) or liner (d43) over it.

failures.detail: An open rust collar (d09) still frames the face. The ecru tee (d03) and navy scarf (d62) only help until the scarf comes off indoors, so the claim that the rust 'stays further down' is wishful.

The brown suede derbies (d50) have crepe soles, which are slippery when wet, and the forecast is passing showers. Grip on the pedals is a directive, not an optional swap. Lead with the lug boots (d55).

A black technical shell (d42) over a charcoal nylon liner (d43) sits on top of a warm rust/ecru/navy look. This is the most technical outerwear stack of the three, and it kills the warmth the look is built on. The olive waxed jacket (d41) would harmonise with the rust.

looks.comment: Right instinct to use the rarely worn rust shirt against navy and ecru, and rolling the sleeves suits his arms. The execution undercuts it: suede-crepe shoes in rain, rust still at the collar, and a black tech shell over a warm palette.

judgement.missedOpportunity: A jacket-ready look that adds warmth: d30 navy unstructured blazer + d12 forest green merino crew + d21 grey flannel trousers + d55 brown lug-sole boots + d65 brown belt + d64 watch, with d41 olive waxed jacket and d63 grey cashmere beanie for the ride. It keeps his proven presentation formula, brings in colour and earthier texture, and is fully rideable in showers. This is what Look 2 should have been.
judgement.summary: Strong opening: Look 1 is exactly what this client needs. It is rideable, textural, warm in colour and quiet, and it unlocks the neglected chocolate cords. Looks 2 and 3 are weaker. Look 2 retreats to the navy-grey formula with filler reasoning and an over-optimistic claim that the blazer survives a backpack ride. Look 3 has the right ambition with the rust shirt but puts slippery crepe-soled suede on wet pedals, overstates how far the rust sits from his face, and smothers its warmth under black technical outerwear. Fix the shoes and outer layer on Look 3, warm up Look 2, and add the beanie before sending.

results.requestText: Dinner with friends at a nice restaurant on Saturday night.

looks.title: Earth and Evergreen
looks.idea: Forest green and chocolate cord: the warm, textured dinner look he never wears, kept quiet.
looks.howToWear: Wear the forest green merino with the sleeves pushed to the forearm, since his long arms make a full-length sleeve look short when pulled down. Leave it untucked at the front only, with a half-tuck at the hip so the brown belt just shows. Let the cord trousers sit with a slight break over the lug-sole boots. Wear the waxed jacket and navy scarf for the ride, then take them off at the restaurant so the green and brown can show.
looks.why: The chocolate cord has only been worn twice, and this is the pairing that makes sense of it. Green and brown sit well with his cool colouring and give him the warmth and texture he says he lacks, with no mustard or orange near his face. The lug boots and waxed jacket handle wind and showers on the bike, and the look still reads as Margaret Howell rather than outdoor gear.

looks.title: Soft Tailoring, Roll-Neck
looks.idea: His proven presentation formula, loosened into an evening look with a soft blazer.
looks.howToWear: Wear the charcoal roll-neck tucked or half-tucked into the flannel trousers, with the black belt. Put the unstructured navy blazer over it with the sleeves just clear of the wrist. Leave the navy scarf loose, not tied. Ride in the rain shell over everything, then stow it in the backpack on arrival so the blazer is what people see.
looks.why: It repeats the charcoal roll-neck, grey flannel and Chelsea boots combination that felt sharp for him. The soft blazer adds a layer of tailoring without the stiffness of the suit that felt over the top. The rubber-soled Chelseas grip the pedals and handle wet pavements, and the blazer has enough shape for a nice restaurant.

looks.title: Cardigan and Pale Blue
looks.idea: A shawl cardigan over a cool blue shirt: relaxed warmth with a precise collar.
looks.howToWear: Wear the pale blue poplin shirt with the top button open and the collar flat over the shawl collar of the oatmeal cardigan. Leave the cardigan open or fastened with one button. Roll the shirt cuffs once under the cardigan sleeve. Tuck the shirt into the navy pleated trousers and wear the brown belt. Wear the waxed jacket on the ride and hang it up at the restaurant.
looks.why: The oatmeal chunky knit brings texture and warmth to navy trousers he already trusts. Pale blue is flattering against his grey-blue eyes. The proportions are relaxed but clean, and none of the pieces is formal enough to look stiff.

output.note: I've assumed you're cycling to dinner, so no look uses the overcoat, the loafers or the Oxfords (slippery on wet pedals). If you're getting a taxi, swap the navy overcoat in for the outerwear in look 2 or 3. I've left the camel suede trucker out because of the showers, and the wardrobe has no waterproof smart layer for it. A mid-weight dark jacket that works on the bike and at dinner would fill that gap.
