failures.detail: For a 'nice restaurant' the look stops at a jumper; the navy unstructured blazer d30 over d12/d26 would lift it to the right register without stiffness.
The tuck instruction is garbled: 'untucked at the front only, with a half-tuck at the hip' contradicts itself. A clean front tuck of fine merino over d65 is what he should be told.

looks.comment: This is the right idea. It finally makes sense of the rarely worn d26 by pairing it with forest green d12 at the face, which answers his wish for warmth and texture, and d55 plus d41 are honest choices for the bike in showers. It needs one more layer and a clearer styling instruction to feel like a nice-restaurant look rather than a good weekend look.

failures.detail: This is his client-presentation outfit (d05+d21+d51) with d30 swapped in for d40, all in navy, charcoal and grey. It reads as a work look on a Saturday and ignores his stated wish to move beyond navy and grey.
The rationale is 'it worked before'. It says nothing about why the look suits an evening out with friends, or how it differs from the studio.

A hip-length black nylon shell d42 over a blazer will crush the soft shoulder and leave the blazer hem hanging below it. The olive waxed jacket d41 sits better over tailoring and isn't technical gear.

looks.comment: Competent and rideable, but it is the presentation uniform re-served, with no evening idea. If it stays as the dressier option, put d41 over it instead of the rain shell, and consider d12 in place of d05 to bring in some colour.

failures.detail: Black Chelsea boots d51 are paired with a brown belt d65 for no stated reason. The oatmeal and navy look wants the brown suede derbies d50 or the brown lug boots d55.
Spreading the shirt collar flat over a shawl collar fights the cardigan. The shawl should frame the shirt collar from outside.
A chunky shawl cardigan d33 under the hip-length waxed jacket d41 will bunch at the shoulders and hem on the ride.
'Pale blue is flattering against his eyes' and 'relaxed but clean' are generic. The thin poplin d02 is also the wrong texture under a chunky knit; the oxford d01 would hold up better.

looks.comment: Oatmeal, pale blue and navy is a pleasant Margaret Howell palette, but the execution is loose: the shoes and belt disagree, the collar instruction is wrong, and the layering doesn't survive the bike.

judgement.missedOpportunity: Put the navy unstructured blazer d30 over the forest green merino d12 with the chocolate cord d26, the brown lug-sole boots d55 (or the brown suede derbies d50 if dry), the brown belt d65 and the watch d64. For the ride, add the olive waxed jacket d41 and navy scarf d62. Navy, forest green and chocolate give a textured, warm, restaurant-ready look that uses his trusted blazer to anchor the under-worn cord.
judgement.summary: Look 1 is a genuinely good find: d26 and d12 together answer Daniel's aspiration for warmth and texture, and the outfit is properly rideable. It falls one layer short of 'nice restaurant'. Look 2 is his presentation uniform recycled in navy and grey, and Look 3 has finishing errors: black boots with a brown belt, a wrong collar move, and a bulky cardigan under the waxed jacket. The stylist's note is honest and useful. It correctly assumes cycling, rules out the loafers and the overcoat, and names the missing smart waterproof layer. Leaving out the camel suede d36 is also right, given the rain and camel near his face. Fix the tuck instruction and add d30 to Look 1, replace the rain shell in Look 2, and rework Look 3 before this goes out.

results.requestText: Surprise me — put together something I wouldn't normally think of.

looks.title: Chocolate and Forest
looks.idea: Brown cord with deep green and a pale blue collar, the warm, earthy version of your navy-and-grey uniform.
looks.howToWear: Wear the pale blue poplin shirt under the forest green merino with only the collar and a thin inch of cuff showing. Leave the shirt untucked at the hem and let the jumper skim the cord waistband. Cuff the cord trousers once so they sit clear of the pedals and over the lug boots. Wear the olive waxed jacket on top with the corduroy collar up against the wind, and the navy scarf tucked inside. Match the brown belt to the boots.
looks.why: The chocolate cord has only been worn twice because it was hard to place. Forest green and pale blue are both in your palette and sit well against your cool colouring, so the brown reads as quiet warmth. It is tonal and textural: cord, merino and waxed cotton. The lug boots grip and shrug off showers, and the cord is easy to pedal in.

looks.title: Rust Over Charcoal
looks.idea: The rust cord shirt worn as a layer over a dark roll-neck, so the colour frames you without sitting at your face.
looks.howToWear: Wear the charcoal roll-neck as the base and the rust corduroy shirt open over it like a light jacket, with the cuffs pushed to the forearm. Leave it untucked, since the relaxed cut is meant to hang. Wear the grey flannel trousers straight over the brown lug boots. Put the black rain shell over everything for the ride and swap the beanie in for the hood. In the studio, take the shell off and the shirt becomes your outer layer.
looks.why: Strong orange sits badly near your face, but rust is muted and the charcoal roll-neck keeps the neckline cool and safe. You get the warmth and texture you want without leaving your palette. It builds on the roll-neck and flannel combination that already worked for you, and the cord shirt has barely been worn. The rain shell is just the outer layer here, not the look.

looks.title: Cream and Black, Softly Tailored
looks.idea: A chunky cream fisherman jumper over black wool trousers, a graphic, high-texture combination.
looks.howToWear: Wear the cream fisherman jumper loose and untucked, with its relaxed length falling over the drawstring waist. Pull the trousers down slightly over the Chelsea boots for one clean line from hip to ground. Add the navy scarf with a single loop and keep the rain shell zipped to the chin on the bike. When you take the shell off, the jumper is the whole top half.
looks.why: Cream is close to the ecru that suits you, and putting it against black gives crisp contrast without any navy or grey. The cable knit and the wool trousers give you the texture you like. The drawstring trousers are easy to pedal in and the Chelsea boots have a rubber sole for grip. It looks relaxed but considered, and it makes use of two pieces you wear less often.

output.note: I left the camel suede trucker out. It is a great piece, but on a windy day with showers it is a risk for a 25-minute ride. Save it for a dry day with ecru chinos or the indigo jeans.

failures.detail: Leaving the d02 poplin untucked under a fine merino d12 crew means shirt tails hang below the jumper hem. That reads sloppy rather than precise on Daniel. Tuck it and let the belt d65 show.
The 'inch of cuff showing' ignores his long arms. Standard d02 sleeves may not clear the merino on him, so this needs a check or a different finishing move.

looks.comment: This is the best look in the set. It finally gives the d26 chocolate cords a home, and it does it with a palette that is fully his: forest green d12, a cool pale-blue d02 collar at the face, the navy d62 scarf and the olive waxed d41. It is rideable, showerproof and very Margaret Howell. Fix the untucked shirt tail and it goes out.

failures.detail: The black technical shell d42 is a default choice. Over rust d09, grey flannel d21 and brown d55 it brings in a hard black that fights the earthy story. The olive waxed d41 is waterproof, has a cord collar and is exactly right here; looks can share outerwear.
The brown belt d65 is listed, but the d05 roll-neck and the open d09 shirt are both untucked, so it does nothing. Either tuck the roll-neck or drop the belt.

looks.comment: Wearing the rust cord shirt open as a light jacket over the charcoal d05 roll-neck is a genuinely clever way to get the hard-to-wear d09 into rotation. The roll-neck keeps orange off his neck, and pushing the sleeves up quietly solves his sleeve-length problem. The one weak point is the commute layer: swap the black shell for the olive waxed d41.

failures.detail: Cream d10 against black d25, d42 and d51 is a high-contrast, warm-white scheme on a low-medium contrast, cool man. Black is not in his palette, and the stark contrast will drain him.
A cream fisherman knit with black trousers is a stock look. It answers neither 'surprise me' nor his aspiration for warmth.
A black belt d66 is listed on drawstring trousers d25, under an untucked chunky knit, so it is redundant. The navy scarf d62 also sits awkwardly between black and cream.
Telling him to pull the trousers down over the Chelsea boots for a long line is the opposite of what he needs on a bike in showers: hems in the chain and soaked flannel-weight wool.
'Cream is close to ecru' glosses over the fact that the black is doing the damage.

looks.comment: This is the weakest look: a generic black-and-cream combination that steps outside his colouring without a reason. It also repeats the black shell d42 as the outer layer for the second time. It does not deliver the surprise or the warmth the brief asked for.

judgement.missedOpportunity: Replace Look 3 with something that is new for him but still in his palette: the navy and white bengal stripe shirt d08 under the oatmeal shawl-collar cardigan d33 (worn as the jacket layer), with olive fatigue trousers d24, brown lug boots d55, the olive waxed jacket d41 for the ride and the grey cashmere beanie d63. It brings pattern and soft texture, and the oatmeal and olive add warmth he never wears together, while keeping cool navy at the face. Separately, Look 2 should use d41 rather than d42.
judgement.summary: This is a good reading of the brief in two of three looks. The stylist went straight for the under-worn d26 chocolate cords and d09 rust shirt, handled the rust-at-the-face risk intelligently, and was honest about why the camel suede d36 stays home in showers. Look 1 is sendable. Look 2 is a smart idea let down by reaching for the black technical shell when the olive waxed jacket would complete it. Look 3 is a generic black-and-cream combination that goes against his low-contrast cool colouring, carries a pointless belt, and gives cycling-unfriendly hem advice. Fix the shell in Look 2 and replace Look 3 before this goes out.

results.requestText: It's raining all day and I'll be walking a lot. What should I wear?

looks.title: Wax, Cord and Cable
looks.idea: Warm, earthy texture in cream, chocolate and olive that is made for wet weather.
looks.howToWear: Wear the cream fisherman jumper untucked under the waxed jacket, with the corduroy collar turned up against the wind. Roll the cord trousers one turn so the hems stay out of the wet and clear of the chain. Wear the navy scarf tucked inside the jacket and keep the brown belt on. Put the backpack on over the jacket.
looks.why: This is the warmth and texture he says he wants, and it gets his under-worn chocolate cords out of the cupboard. Cream by the face suits his cool colouring, and the waxed jacket gives real waterproofing without looking like outdoor kit. The lug boots grip on wet pedals and pavements and keep his feet dry on a long walk.

looks.title: Green Flannel Under the Shell
looks.idea: A quiet, layered look in forest green, navy and grey that does the work in bad weather.
looks.howToWear: Wear the navy merino crew as the base layer, with the green flannel overshirt open over it like a light jacket. Wear the black shell over both and zip it fully, with the hood up only when the wind demands it. Wear the grey flannel trousers straight and slightly cuffed over the Chelsea boots. Keep the cashmere beanie in a pocket and put it on under the hood in the gusts.
looks.why: Forest green is one of his best colours and he rarely uses it, so it brings colour into his navy and grey. The wool layers stay warm even when damp, and the shell is the only technical piece, so it never becomes a full outdoor look. The Chelsea boots have a rubber sole for grip and are sharp enough for the studio.

looks.title: Shawl-Collar Studio Walker
looks.idea: Soft tailoring in pale blue, oatmeal and navy, with a waterproof shell kept on top.
looks.howToWear: Wear the pale blue poplin shirt with the collar open and the sleeves pushed up once, so his long arms don't leave the cuffs short. Wear the oatmeal shawl cardigan over it, and the navy pleated trousers belted with the brown belt. Wear the black shell over everything with the scarf tucked in. Take the shell off at the studio and the look still stands on its own.
looks.why: It is the most polished option and still relaxed, close to the spirit of his navy-merino-and-pleated-trousers uniform. The oatmeal cardigan adds warmth and texture, and the pale blue shirt is flattering against his grey-blue eyes. The wool trousers and tapered leg cope with the weather and are easy to pedal in.

output.note: I assumed you might be on the bike, so every look has grip-soled shoes, a hip-length outer layer and trousers you can pedal in. The overcoat, the loafers, the suede trainers and the camel suede jacket are left out because they suit this weather badly. If you have a client presentation today, look 3 with the navy blazer swapped for the cardigan is the closest fit, though the wardrobe has no shell that goes over a blazer neatly.

failures.detail: d26 wide-wale cotton cord sits below the hip-length d41 for a full day of heavy rain. It will soak, sag and stay cold, because cotton loses warmth when wet where wool does not. The look is worth sending, but it needs a line telling him to expect wet shins or to keep these cords for a drier day.

'Keep the brown belt on' under an untucked chunky d10 is filler. The explanation never names the best thing in the look: d41's corduroy collar echoes the d26 cord. It also says nothing about sleeve length on his long arms with a relaxed fisherman knit.

looks.comment: The strongest look and the one with a real point of view. It answers his warmth-and-texture aspiration, rescues the unworn d26, and uses the only genuinely rainproof jacket (d41) and boots (d55) in the wardrobe. The navy d62 at the throat keeps one of his own colours near the face. Its only real flaw is cotton cord trousers exposed to a whole day of rain.

failures.detail: The whole idea is forest green d34, but it is zipped under the black d42 shell for an all-day walk in the rain. Outdoors, the look reads as black shell, grey trousers and black boots: the navy-and-grey he is trying to escape.

Black Chelsea boots d51 have elastic side gussets that wick water on long wet walks, while d55 is explicitly rainproof. Cuffing the grey flannel d21 creates a turn-up that collects water. The look also skips d43, the liner made for wearing under the shell in 5°C wind.
Apart from the overshirt, this is his usual navy and grey. The brown belt d65 is pointlessly mismatched with black boots, shell and bag when d66 exists, although it is hidden.

looks.comment: Competent layering with a sensible idea, using his best under-used colour (green). The execution buries that colour under the least characterful outer layer in the wardrobe. Putting d34 under d41 instead, or adding d43 under d42, would have made the look either more visible or warmer.

failures.detail: A chunky shawl-collar cardigan d33 under a fitted hip-length technical shell d42 crushes the collar and bunches at the hem. The cardigan is the whole point of the look, and it does not survive the commute.
This is not a known miss, but it repeats Look 2's shell, boots and bag and stays in navy territory. The range across the three looks is narrower than it appears.

Calling it 'soft tailoring' is wrong: there is no tailored piece in the look. Pushing up the poplin sleeves 'so long arms don't leave the cuffs short' makes no sense under knit sleeves and a shell at 5°C. 'Tapered leg copes with the weather' is not a reason.

Chelsea boots d51 are again chosen over the rainproof lug d55 for a day of walking in heavy rain. Thin poplin under an open-front cardigan is also cold at the chest once the shell comes off in a draughty studio.

looks.comment: Pleasant indoors, since pale blue, oatmeal and navy suit him, but it is barely a step away from his uniform and is not built for the brief. The best part of the whole proposal is the honest note about the missing blazer-friendly shell.

judgement.missedOpportunity: A green-led wet-weather look that keeps colour at the face and wool on the legs: d05 charcoal lambswool roll-neck (replaces the scarf against the wind), d34 forest green flannel overshirt, d41 olive waxed jacket with the cord collar up, d21 grey flannel trousers (wool stays warm when damp), d55 brown lug-sole boots, d63 grey cashmere beanie, d60, d64. It is tonal green-on-olive over charcoal and grey, adds texture without leaving his palette, and every piece suits rain, wind and the bike.
judgement.summary: Look 1 is genuinely good: it reaches for the waxed jacket, the lug boots and the neglected chocolate cords, and it delivers the warmth and texture Daniel asked for. Looks 2 and 3 both default to the black technical shell and side-gusset Chelsea boots for a day of walking in heavy rain. Look 2 hides its green under the shell; Look 3 crushes its cardigan under it and drifts back into his navy uniform. The rideability assumption and the note on the absent blazer-compatible shell are sensible and honest. The stylist should have used d55 and d41 more than once and reconsidered putting cotton cord in the wettest zone. Send Look 1 with a note about wet shins; rework the other two.

results.requestText: First date — cocktails at a smart bar.

looks.title: Forest and Flannel
looks.idea: Quiet colour on the face, with a soft navy blazer to keep it sharp.
looks.howToWear: Wear the forest green merino crew with the navy unstructured blazer over it and leave the blazer open. Push the blazer sleeves up slightly so your long arms don't look cramped. Keep the grey flannel straight and let it break just on top of the Chelsea boots. Wear the black belt to match the boots. Put the olive waxed jacket over everything for the ride and the wind, with the navy scarf tucked inside. Take the jacket and scarf off at the bar.
looks.why: Forest green is one of your best colours and gives you the warmth you want without leaving navy and grey. The unlined blazer reads polished but relaxed, which is closer to your 'considered, not tried' brief than the stiff suit that didn't work. The rubber-soled Chelsea boots grip the pedals and handle wet streets, and the waxed jacket is waterproof without looking like technical gear.

looks.title: Chocolate and Charcoal
looks.idea: A texture-led, low-key look in deep tones, with corduroy bringing the warmth.
looks.howToWear: Wear the charcoal lambswool roll-neck with the chocolate wide-wale cords, and add the navy blazer on top as a sharp third layer. Wear the brown belt only if the roll-neck is tucked in at the front. Otherwise leave it untucked and skip the belt. Let the relaxed cord leg sit over the top of the lug-sole boots, with a small cuff if it catches the chain. Wear the waxed jacket and scarf outside for the ride.
looks.why: This finally gives the under-worn chocolate cords a job. Brown, navy and charcoal is a rich, grown-up combination, and the roll-neck was already your most successful look for a sharp occasion. The roll-neck sits well on a long frame and the texture reads as warm and confident. The lug-sole boots grip and keep the rain out, and the dark palette hides any damp from the ride.

looks.title: Soft Cardigan, Crisp Shirt
looks.idea: Relaxed knitwear over a pale blue shirt, for an easy, approachable first impression.
looks.howToWear: Wear the pale blue poplin shirt with the collar open and the top button undone. Cuff it once, loosely, to deal with the sleeve length. Put the oatmeal shawl-collar cardigan over it and let the shawl collar sit open and slightly rolled. Wear the navy pleated trousers with the brown belt and the brown suede derbies. Wear the waxed jacket and scarf for the ride. If the showers are heavy, swap the derbies for the lug-sole boots (d55).
looks.why: Pale blue and oatmeal flatter your cool colouring and add real softness and texture, which is the warmth you said you're missing. The pleated navy trousers are your proven staple, now dressed up with a better shirt. The shawl cardigan keeps it approachable and a little more relaxed than a blazer. The crepe-sole derbies give grip, though the suede does need the swap above in a downpour.

output.note: I've kept all three looks rideable, with no overcoat and no slippery loafers, since you'll probably cycle. If you take a taxi instead, the navy overcoat (d40) would work well over any of them. I left the camel suede jacket out because of the showers, and the tie stays at home.

failures.detail: 'Push the blazer sleeves up' on a tailored wool blazer (d30) at a smart bar looks sloppy and creases the sleeve. The better fix for his long arms is a slim shirt or knit cuff showing at the wrist, or simply leaving the sleeve as it is. The note also never says what to do with the black roll-top (d60) at the bar.
This is essentially his winter presentation formula (d21 + d51 + jacket) with d12 swapped in for d05. It is correct, but it reads closer to client meeting than first date.

looks.comment: A solid, rideable and flattering look. d12 at the face adds the warmth he asked for, and d41 over d30 handles wind and showers without looking technical. The sleeve-pushing instruction should be cut, and there is little here that says 'date' rather than 'presentation'.

failures.detail: Charcoal d05, chocolate d26 and navy d30 are three dark mid-value neutrals with no light point. In a dim cocktail bar, on a low-contrast man, this goes muddy rather than 'rich'. The navy blazer over chocolate also creates a dark-on-dark seam that neither contrasts nor matches.
Wide-wale cord (formality 2) plus chunky lug-sole boots d55 (formality 2) pull the bottom half towards weekend-with-the-kids, not smart bar. The blazer is fighting the lower half.
'The roll-neck was already your most successful look for a sharp occasion' borrows credit from a different outfit. Calling this palette rich does not test whether the three darks actually separate.

looks.comment: The instinct is right: finally giving the neglected d26 a job is exactly what this wardrobe needs. The execution is off. Swap d05 for d12 (forest green) or d10 (cream), and in dry weather go to d50, and this becomes the best look in the set.

failures.detail: A chunky oatmeal shawl cardigan d33 over poplin reads cosy-fireside or studio Friday, not cocktails at a smart bar on a first date. It undershoots the room.
d20 navy pleated trousers plus d50 brown suede derbies is literally his studio uniform. A date look built on his work base is not an occasion look.
Brown suede derbies d50 are recommended in a forecast of passing showers on a bike. The stylist half-concedes this with a swap to d55, which then makes the look even more casual.
A chunky shawl cardigan under the hip-length waxed jacket d41 adds bulk across the torso and collar on the ride. The shawl collar will also crush under the jacket.

looks.comment: Pleasant colour at the face, but it is the wrong energy for a smart bar and recycles his weekday uniform. If a knit-over-shirt idea was wanted, d12 over d02 under d30 with d21 would have stayed on register.

judgement.missedOpportunity: d12 forest green merino + d26 chocolate wide-wale cords + d30 navy unstructured blazer + d50 brown suede derbies in dry spells, or d55 if raining + d65 brown belt + d64 watch, with d41 waxed jacket and d62 scarf for the ride. It puts his best warm-cool colour at the face, finally uses the cords with a partner that separates from them, and delivers the 'more warmth and texture' aspiration in a register that suits a smart bar.
judgement.summary: Competent, practical and rideable throughout. The weather and the cycling directive are respected, the tie is correctly left home, and it is right to avoid both the rust shirt d09 near his face and the suede trucker d36 in showers. Look 1 is sendable. Look 2 has the right idea in the under-worn chocolate cords but pairs them into a muddy, dark-on-dark palette with boots too casual for the room. Look 3 is his studio uniform with a cardigan, under-pitched for a first date and risky in suede. All three share identical outerwear, scarf and bag, so the range is narrower than it looks. Nobody addresses arriving at a date with a cycling backpack, or offers a plan B if he takes a taxi beyond the overcoat swap. The clearest gain is putting d12 with d26 under d30, which would have been the standout look.

results.requestText: Weekend brunch and then wandering around the shops.

looks.title: Chocolate and Cream
looks.idea: The cords he never knows how to wear, in a warm, textured, tonal brown-and-cream look.
looks.howToWear: Wear the cream fisherman jumper loose over the cords, untucked, with the sleeves pushed to the forearm. Its length and relaxed fit suit his long arms. Add the brown belt for a quiet line at the waist. The waxed jacket goes on top with the corduroy collar up against the wind, and the navy scarf sits tucked inside it. Keep the trouser hem straight over the lug boots with no break.
looks.why: It gives him the warmth and texture he's asking for and moves off navy and grey. Cream is an ecru-family shade that suits his cool colouring, and the navy scarf by his face keeps it grounded. The cords are warm, the waxed jacket and rainproof boots handle showers, and the lug soles grip the pedals if he cycles. It's relaxed enough for brunch with the kids and still looks precise.

looks.title: Green Overshirt, Indigo Denim
looks.idea: A weekend uniform built on forest green and ecru, with sharp contrast in textures.
looks.howToWear: Wear the forest green flannel overshirt open over the ecru heavyweight tee, with the tee untucked at the front only. Roll the jeans one clean turn at the hem to show the Chelsea boots. Wear the grey cashmere beanie and the black belt. Keep the rain shell in the backpack and put it over the overshirt when a shower comes. It's fine zipped over the top, because the overshirt and jeans carry the look.
looks.why: Forest green and ecru are both in his best palette, and green sits well against his grey-blue eyes. The brushed flannel and raw denim add the texture he likes without any logos. The shell is practical cover and not the whole outfit, so it doesn't turn into a technical-gear look. Everything is rideable and weatherproof enough for the shops.

looks.title: Cardigan and Flannel
looks.idea: The tailored, softened version of his studio look, for a slower weekend.
looks.howToWear: Open the oatmeal shawl-collar cardigan over the pale blue poplin shirt and leave the top button undone, with no tie. Tuck the shirt in and wear the black belt. Let the flannel trousers sit straight over the Chelsea boots. Put the navy overcoat on top for the walk between shops, with the scarf looped once inside the collar. Carry the brown briefcase if he's bringing anything for the studio.
looks.why: It builds on the charcoal-roll-neck, flannel and overcoat combination that worked for him before, now with oatmeal and pale blue for warmth and softness. Pale blue is a cool tone that flatters him, and the chunky cardigan adds texture to an otherwise quiet palette. The overcoat is long, so on a cycling day swap it for the olive waxed jacket (d41) and carry the black backpack (d60) instead of the briefcase.

output.note: I left out the rust cord shirt (d09) and the camel suede jacket (d36). Rust sits too close to the warm tones that don't suit him near his face, and suede in passing showers is a risk. The rust shirt would only work as an open layer over ecru, away from his face.

failures.detail: 'Its length and relaxed fit suit his long arms' doesn't hold up. Pushing the d10 sleeves up is a fix for sleeves that run short, which is a good move, but the note should say so rather than claim the fit suits him.

The d65 brown belt goes under an untucked chunky fisherman knit, so it can't create the 'quiet line at the waist' it is credited with. Either half-tuck the front of d10 so the belt shows or drop the line.

A chunky cable knit (d10) under a hip-length waxed jacket (d41) risks bulk in the sleeves and the knit hem poking out below the jacket. Check the lengths and tell him to tug the knit down flat before zipping.

looks.comment: This is the best look in the set. It finally gives the rarely worn d26 cords a job, answers his wish for warmth and texture, and the d41 waxed jacket with the d55 lug boots handles wind, showers and the bike. The navy d62 scarf at the face is the right buffer for cream, and the whole thing reads Margaret Howell rather than costume. The styling notes just need tightening.

failures.detail: At 6°C and windy, a flannel overshirt (d34) over a tee (d03) is underdressed. The d42 shell stays in the bag until it rains and adds almost no warmth when it is on. The d43 quilted liner exists precisely to go under the shell and is ignored.
This is his most-worn weekend kit (d23 worn 22x, d03 18x, d34 10x) restated. It adds nothing to the aspiration of more warmth and texture beyond the green he already wears.
'Untucked at the front only' is muddled; it should presumably be a front half-tuck. The d66 black belt is then mostly hidden. 'Wear the beanie and the black belt' is a list, not styling.
Claiming the zipped black shell is fine 'because the overshirt and jeans carry the look' ignores that the shell covers the overshirt entirely whenever it is on.

looks.comment: The palette logic is sound, since forest green and ecru are among his best colours, but the look is cold for the forecast and is simply his usual weekend outfit. To make it work, swap d03 for the d12 forest green merino crew under d34, or add d43 under d42. Better still, use the d41 waxed jacket so the outer layer is part of the look.

failures.detail: A tucked poplin shirt (d02), flannels (d21), the d40 overcoat and a brief case (d61) is studio dress for a weekend brunch and shopping. 'If he's bringing anything for the studio' misreads the brief entirely.
The default outer layer is the knee-length d40, which is noted as awkward on the bike. The cycling swap is pushed into a footnote, so the look as presented is not rideable.
A chunky shawl-collar cardigan (d33) under a single-breasted overcoat (d40) makes a bulky, crowded neckline. It is also impractical for trying things on in shops.
Shopping wearing three heavy layers plus a briefcase, while possibly with the kids, is a real-life miss.

looks.comment: The colour at the face works: pale blue for his cool colouring with oatmeal for softness. But it is a rerun of his winter presentation look dressed down slightly, pitched too formal for the occasion and not rideable as presented. Rebuild it around d41 and d55, with d23 or d26 instead of d21, and drop the briefcase.

judgement.missedOpportunity: The stylist dismissed d09 because rust sits near the face, but that problem can be solved. Wear the d09 rust needlecord shirt open as a light jacket over the d12 forest green merino crew, so green sits at the neck and the navy d62 scarf buffers the collar. Add the d23 raw selvedge jeans, d55 lug boots and the d41 waxed jacket on top, with the d64 watch, d65 belt and d60 backpack. This gives him real warmth and colour away from navy and grey, uses a piece bought for that purpose and worn only twice, and is rideable and showerproof.
judgement.summary: Look 1 is strong and on-brief: the d26 cords, finally styled, the d10 cream fisherman knit with the d62 navy scarf at the face, and the d41 waxed jacket with d55 boots for the weather and the bike. Fix the hidden belt and the sleeve reasoning and it can go. Look 2 is his existing weekend uniform and is underdressed for 6°C and wind, with the d43 liner and d12 merino both ignored. Look 3 is studio dress transplanted to a weekend: an overcoat as default that breaks the cycling directive, a briefcase for brunch, and a bulky cardigan under a coat. The stylist was right to keep the suede d36 out of the showers, but too timid to solve the rust shirt d09, which is the piece that would most directly answer his request for more warmth. One excellent look and two that need rework: send Look 1 now, and revise Looks 2 and 3.

results.requestText: I'm presenting to senior leadership next week. I want to look authoritative but still like me.

looks.title: The Sharpened Uniform
looks.idea: Your proven presentation formula, with a soft navy jacket added so the roll-neck reads as authority rather than just warmth.
looks.howToWear: Wear the charcoal roll-neck untucked under the unstructured navy blazer, with the neck folded once so it sits cleanly against the blazer collar. Push the jumper sleeves up an inch or two so the length reads deliberate rather than short. Let the grey flannel trousers break just once over the brown suede derbies, and keep the brown belt in the loops even though the jumper covers it. Ride in the waxed jacket and navy scarf, then take both off at the studio so the blazer is the outermost layer in the room.
looks.why: It repeats the winter presentation look that felt sharp, but the blazer adds the structure a senior-leadership room expects. The tonal charcoal, navy and grey are your best colours near your face. The lambswool, flannel and suede give texture, which is your signature. The waxed jacket keeps the look rideable and waterproof in the showers, and the crepe sole grips the pedals.

looks.title: Warm Tones, Still Quiet
looks.idea: The most 'you with more warmth' option: forest green and chocolate cord under a navy blazer, tailored enough to command the room.
looks.howToWear: Wear the pale blue poplin shirt under the forest green merino crew, with the collar out over the knit and the cuffs just showing at the wrists, which also helps with your long arms. Add the navy blazer over the top. Keep the chocolate wide-wale cords clean-lined with a slight break over the lug-sole boots, and wear the brown belt. Ride in the waxed jacket, then take it off at the studio.
looks.why: This finally puts the rarely-worn chocolate cords to work. Brown, green and pale blue are all cool-friendly and give you the extra warmth and texture you asked for, with no rust or mustard near your face. The navy blazer and the shirt-and-knit layering keep it authoritative. The lug-sole boots are rainproof and grip on the bike, so the weather is covered.

looks.title: Broken Suit, Softened
looks.idea: Authority from the charcoal jacket, with its stiffness undone by mixing in different textures and a warm green layer.
looks.howToWear: Wear the charcoal suit jacket without its matching trousers, and put it with the lighter mid-grey flannel instead. Layer the pale blue poplin shirt under the forest green merino crew, with the collar out and the shirt cuffs peeking from the knit. Wear the black belt with the black Chelsea boots, and keep the trouser break clean and slightly high so the boots show. Ride in the waxed jacket over the suit jacket and the scarf, and take them off on arrival.
looks.why: This gives you the most formal jacket in the wardrobe without repeating the stiff full-suit look that felt over the top. The flannel and the green knit break up the suiting. It reads precise and senior, but still tactile and personal. The rubber-soled Chelsea boots are rideable and handle wet pavements.

output.note: I've assumed you'll cycle in, so every look uses the waxed jacket and the backpack, and I've left out the leather-soled loafers and Oxfords because they're slippery on wet pedals. If you're not riding that day, swap the waxed jacket for the navy overcoat and the backpack for the brown briefcase for extra polish. No tie is needed in any of these looks, and the burgundy tie stays in the drawer. The one gap is a smart mid-length coat that works on a bike. The overcoat is the only formal outer layer and it's awkward to pedal in, so on riding days the waxed jacket is the best compromise.

failures.detail: Swaps the proven black Chelsea boots (d51, rubber sole) for brown suede derbies (d50) on a day of passing showers. That means wet suede before an important presentation, and a crepe sole that gets slick on wet pedals. The stylist's claim that it 'grips the pedals' is wrong.

'Push the jumper sleeves up an inch or two' is not a usable move under a blazer. The knit just bunches inside the jacket sleeve. Daniel's long-arm problem is the blazer's sleeve length, and that isn't addressed at all.
Charcoal, grey and navy is exactly the 'lives in navy and grey' palette he wants to move beyond. It's right as the safe anchor, but it adds nothing new.

looks.comment: This is the correct backbone: his proven d05/d21 formula with the d30 blazer added for authority. The shoe swap undermines it, though. Keep d51 with d66 as in the look that worked, and drop the sleeve-pushing advice.

failures.detail: Wide-wale cord (d26, formality 2) and chunky lug-sole boots (d55, formality 2) pull the look into weekend territory. That's the wrong register for 'authoritative' in front of senior leadership. The soft d30 blazer can't lift it alone.
Calls chocolate brown 'cool-friendly', which it isn't. It works here only because it sits away from the face. The explanation should say that.

looks.comment: This is a genuinely good use of the neglected d26 and d12, and it answers his warmth-and-texture aspiration in a Margaret Howell way. It's better for a studio day or a dinner than for this presentation. The navy, green, pale blue, chocolate and olive mix also starts to feel busy.

failures.detail: An orphaned smooth worsted suit jacket (d31) over mid-grey flannel (d21) puts two close greys with mismatched cloth next to each other. It reads as 'lost the suit trousers', not as a deliberate odd-jacket pairing.
The structured d31 is the piece behind his known stiff-suit miss. Its rigid shoulder fights his soft, Lemaire/Our Legacy taste even when broken up.
A structured jacket layered under a hip-length waxed jacket (d41) on a 25-minute ride will bulk up, crease and likely hang below the hem.

looks.comment: The instinct to borrow authority from d31 is understandable, but the execution feels like someone else's wardrobe. It also copies Look 2's top half (d02 + d12) exactly. The d30 blazer in place of d31 would have made this the strongest look in the set.

judgement.missedOpportunity: d30 navy unstructured blazer + d12 forest green merino crew (over d02 pale blue poplin, collar sitting cleanly at the crew neck) + d21 grey flannel trousers + d51 black Chelsea boots + d66 black belt + d64 watch; ride in d41 with d62 and d63 against the wind. This combines the authority of his proven presentation formula with the green warmth he wants near his face, and the shoes are rain-safe and grip on the bike.
judgement.summary: The logistics are thought through: the cycling assumption, the overcoat/briefcase swap, the tie ruled out, and an honest note about the missing bike-friendly smart coat. The styling itself is uneven. Look 1 is the right answer but trades rain-proof Chelsea boots for suede, and gives unworkable sleeve advice. Look 2 smartly activates the neglected cords and green knit, but at the wrong formality for senior leadership. Look 3 orphans a worsted suit jacket against flannel and revives the stiffness he rejected. The best look sits between the three, using d30, d12 and d21 with d51, and the stylist never assembled it. The long-arm issue is the blazer sleeve, and it goes unaddressed.

results.requestText: Wedding guest — outdoor afternoon ceremony, and the forecast says it might rain.

looks.title: Green and Navy, Quietly Warm
looks.idea: Your navy-and-grey base with forest green brought up to your face, so it reads as a wedding guest and not as the studio uniform.
looks.howToWear: Wear the forest green merino crew under the unlined navy blazer, with the blazer open. Keep the grey flannel trousers straight, with a clean break over the Chelsea boots, and wear the black belt. Wear the overcoat over everything for the outdoor ceremony and tuck the navy scarf inside the lapels against the wind. Take the coat off once you're inside. Push the blazer sleeves up slightly only if they ride short on your long arms.
looks.why: Forest green is one of your best colours against cool, grey-blue colouring, and it adds the warmth you're missing without breaking the tailored, textural look. The soft, unlined blazer keeps it relaxed. Flannel and wool give texture in the cold. Rubber-soled Chelseas cope with wet grass and pavement far better than leather-soled shoes or suede. This is the same recipe as your winter presentation look, with green in place of charcoal.

looks.title: Cord and Cable, Rain-Ready
looks.idea: A textured, earthy look for a relaxed wedding, using the corduroy trousers you never know how to wear.
looks.howToWear: Wear the pale blue poplin shirt with the collar open and no tie, under the oatmeal shawl-collar cardigan, so the collar sits neatly inside the shawl. Wear the chocolate cord trousers with the brown belt and let them stack slightly over the lug-sole boots. Put the olive waxed jacket over the top for the ceremony, with its corduroy collar turned up. Once indoors, the cardigan alone looks dressed enough.
looks.why: Pale blue is cool and flattering, and the chocolate, oatmeal and olive stay in a warm, muted palette that suits you. It is the most texture-led, Margaret Howell-style option, and it puts two under-worn pieces to use. The waxed jacket and rainproof, grippy boots cover the forecast and the walk across a field. It is the most casual of the three, so it suits a relaxed or country wedding, not a formal venue.

looks.title: Suit, Loosened
looks.idea: The charcoal suit worn like you, with a roll-neck instead of a shirt, so it feels tonal and easy and not stiff.
looks.howToWear: Wear the charcoal lambswool roll-neck under the suit jacket, with the jacket unbuttoned or fastened at one button. Wear the black belt, even though the roll-neck mostly hides it. Wear the trousers straight with a slight break over the Chelsea boots, not Oxfords. Put the navy overcoat over the top for the outdoor ceremony and drop it inside.
looks.why: This is the formal option, and it avoids the mistake of the stiff suit lunch: no white Oxford shirt, no Oxford shoes and no tie, just tonal charcoal with soft lambswool texture. The roll-neck is the warmest option for a windy 6°C afternoon. It echoes the charcoal roll-neck, charcoal flannel and Chelsea combination that felt sharp at your winter presentation.

output.note: There's no umbrella in the wardrobe, so bring one for the ceremony. The navy overcoat in looks 1 and 3 is too long to cycle in, so on a bike swap it for the olive waxed jacket (d41) and carry the blazer or suit jacket in the briefcase or backpack. I've kept the black penny loafers and Oxfords out because leather soles are slippery in the wet.

failures.detail: 'Push the blazer sleeves up slightly if they ride short' is the wrong fix for a wedding. The answer to Daniel's long arms is a shirt cuff showing below the d30 sleeve. Layering d02 pale blue poplin under d12, collar out, would do that and lift the crew neck into wedding register.
It calls this 'the same recipe as your winter presentation look, with green in place of charcoal'. That look was a roll-neck with no blazer, so the comparison is inaccurate filler.
A bare crew neck under a blazer is studio smart-casual. Nothing here marks the occasion beyond the colour swap.

looks.comment: This is the right instinct: d12 forest green at the face answers his warmth aspiration, and d30, d21 and d51 handle the weather and register reasonably. It needs d02's collar and cuffs under the crew, not pushed-up blazer sleeves, before it is a wedding look rather than a nice studio day.

failures.detail: Once d41 comes off indoors, a chunky d33 shawl cardigan over poplin with d55 lug boots is underdressed for a wedding guest, even a relaxed one. Saying 'the cardigan alone looks dressed enough' is not true for this occasion.
It rescues d26 by pushing it into weekend territory. It should have shown the cords working under tailoring: d30 over them is the obvious, stronger move.

looks.comment: The palette is lovely and genuinely his: pale blue, oatmeal, chocolate and olive is exactly the warmth he wants. But this is a weekend-pub outfit, not a wedding-guest outfit, and the caveat doesn't excuse sending it for this brief.

failures.detail: Head-to-toe charcoal (d31, d32, d05) with black d51 and a navy d40 is the darkest possible answer from a client who says he lives in navy and grey and wants more warmth. It is also slightly sombre for a wedding.
There is no d62 scarf for a windy 6°C outdoor ceremony, although Look 1 includes it.

It cites 'charcoal flannel' from the presentation look, but those trousers were mid-grey d21. It also never addresses whether the invitation might actually call for a tie, where d67 with d02 under the suit would be the honest fallback.

looks.comment: This is the correct formal hedge, and the roll-neck under the suit is a sound way to avoid the stiff-suit miss while staying warm. It is tonal to the point of flat, though, and does nothing for his aspiration.

judgement.missedOpportunity: d30 navy unstructured blazer + d02 pale blue poplin shirt under d12 forest green merino crew (collar and cuffs showing, which solves the long arms) + d26 chocolate wide-wale cords + d55 brown lug-sole boots + d65 brown belt + d64 watch + d62 navy scarf, under d40 for the ceremony (or d41 if cycling). That puts the neglected cords under tailoring, brings green and brown warmth to a cool colouring without leaving his navy anchor, and is properly dressed for a relaxed wedding while staying rain- and grass-proof.
judgement.summary: Competent and practical, and the weather handling is right: rubber or lug soles, leather soles excluded, an umbrella flagged, and the overcoat-versus-bike problem addressed. But looks 1 and 3 share the same overcoat, Chelseas, black belt and watch frame, so range is thin. Look 2 is a nice outfit pitched at the wrong occasion. The stylist correctly spotted the levers: green at the face, the unworn cords, and his warmth aspiration. However, they never combined them under a jacket, which is where this wardrobe's best wedding answer lies. Small finishing errors need cutting before this goes out: pushed-up blazer sleeves, a missing scarf, a misremembered past look, and no word on a tie if the invitation requires one.

results.requestText: How should I wear my camel suede trucker jacket (d36)?

looks.title: Camel, Forest and Flannel
looks.idea: The trucker as a warm, textured counterpoint to cool green and grey, which is the first step out of navy.
looks.howToWear: Wear the forest green merino crew straight over the trousers with the hem left out, so it sits just below the trucker's cropped hem. Don't layer a shirt under it. Push the knit sleeves to the forearm so any sleeve length mismatch looks deliberate, and let a little knit show at the trucker's cuff. Zip or snap the jacket closed against the wind and tuck the navy scarf in under the collar. Wear the brown lug-sole boots over the flannel hem, with the brown belt to match.
looks.why: Forest green is one of his best colours and sits against his face, so the camel stays at the jacket and doesn't compete with his cool colouring. Grey flannel keeps it studio-smart, and the suede, merino and flannel give the texture he's after. The lug boots grip the pedals and handle the showers, and the straight trousers are fine to pedal in.

looks.title: Tonal Earth with Cream
looks.idea: Camel, chocolate and cream in one warm, tactile palette that finally gives the corduroy trousers a reason to be worn.
looks.howToWear: Pull the chunky cream fisherman jumper over the cords and leave it loose. The trucker's cropped hem lets the jumper's cable-knit hem show underneath, so the layers read as three stacked textures. Fold the navy scarf once and tuck it in at the neck, which cools the palette near his face. Add the grey cashmere beanie for the ride and take it off at the studio. Wear the brown lug-sole boots with the cords falling straight over them, and the brown belt.
looks.why: Chocolate corduroy, camel suede and cream wool is the warmth and texture he says he's missing, and it fits the Margaret Howell / Norse Projects references. Cream is close to ecru, which flatters him, and the navy scarf adds a cool note near his face. This is the best use of the underworn cords. The jumper adds enough insulation under an unlined suede jacket in 6°C wind, and the relaxed cords are easy to pedal in.

looks.title: Indigo, Charcoal and Camel
looks.idea: A sharper weekday take on denim and suede, with a roll-neck to keep it precise.
looks.howToWear: Tuck nothing: wear the charcoal roll-neck loose over the raw indigo jeans, with the hem just clearing the belt. Fold the roll-neck once, loosely, to show the texture at the collar. Wear the trucker open or snapped at the collar only, since the roll-neck fills the neckline. Leave the jeans unrolled or with one narrow cuff so the Chelsea boots stay visible. Wear the black Chelsea boots and the brown belt.
looks.why: Charcoal and indigo are cool and low-contrast, so they work with his colouring, and camel suede is the one warm piece between them. It repeats the charcoal roll-neck and Chelsea boot formula that worked for him, in a more relaxed form. The straight jeans suit his build, and the rubber-soled Chelsea boots grip the pedals.

output.note: Suede and showers: nothing here is waterproof on top. Treat the jacket with a suede protector spray before wearing it, keep the black rain shell (d42) in the roll-top backpack, and put it on over the trucker if a shower catches you on the bike. The shell is hip length, so it will cover the cropped jacket. On a wet commute, the olive waxed jacket (d41) is the better choice, and the trucker is best for dry days or the studio and dinners. The wardrobe has no other suede-friendly outer layer, so this is the honest limit.

failures.detail: The sleeve instruction contradicts itself. It says to push the d12 knit sleeves to the forearm and also to let knit show at the d36 cuff, which can't both happen under a jacket. The real fix for his long arms is to let the merino cuff extend past the suede cuff by about 1cm, so the short sleeve reads as layered.
'Wear the brown lug-sole boots over the flannel hem' is unclear. It should say the flannel breaks cleanly over the d55 boots, not that the trousers are stuffed into them.

looks.comment: This is the right first look. Forest green d12 keeps his best colour at the face, grey flannel d21 keeps it studio-smart, and camel d36 brings the warmth with no clash, so it is a sharper Daniel rather than a new one. The navy scarf d62 slightly undercuts the 'first step out of navy' idea, but it earns its place against the wind, and the sleeve instruction needs rewriting.

failures.detail: The chunky relaxed cable d10 under a fitted cropped trucker d36 will bunch in the sleeves and push them up his long arms. The jumper hem also drops loose below the jacket, so the three-tier stack risks looking bulky rather than deliberate. It needs a note to wear the trucker open and let the cable hem sit no more than a hand's width below the jacket.

looks.comment: This is the most valuable look in the set. It finally gives the chocolate cords d26 a reason to exist and delivers exactly the warmth and texture he asked for, and the navy scarf d62 cooling the face is a smart, explained move. The cost is bulk: a fully warm palette with chunky cable under suede edges toward heavy on a lean 188cm frame.

failures.detail: The jeans d23 (worn 22x) with a trucker is the most obvious answer, and the 'sharper' idea rests only on the roll-neck d05.

The leathers are muddled. A visible brown belt d65 ('hem just clearing the belt') sits with black Chelsea boots d51 and a black backpack d60, and this isn't addressed. Either hide the belt fully or switch to the black belt d66.
There is no scarf or hat at 6°C in wind, unlike the other two looks, and the long-arm sleeve issue isn't mentioned.

looks.comment: This look is competent and cool-toned, and the link to his proven roll-neck and Chelsea look is a fair argument. However, it is the least considered of the three, and the mixed brown and black leathers would undermine the 'precise' brief he cares about.

judgement.missedOpportunity: A bridge between Looks 1 and 2: d36 camel suede trucker + d12 forest green merino + d26 chocolate cords + d55 lug boots + d63 grey beanie + d64. This uses both underworn pieces (d12 and d26) at once, keeps a cool colour he wears well at the face, and avoids the bulk of the fisherman jumper under the trucker.
judgement.summary: This is a solid, honest answer to a real request. Looks 1 and 2 find good homes for the trucker, and Look 2 cleverly rescues the unworn chocolate cords. The stylist's note on rain is exactly right: protector spray, the d42 shell packed in the backpack, and d41 waxed cotton for wet commutes. That plainly names the jacket's limits, which addresses his actual worry. Weaknesses: the long-arm sleeve problem with a trucker is only half-addressed and the instruction contradicts itself, Look 2's chunky knit under the trucker isn't proportion-managed, and Look 3 is a safe denim default with a careless brown and black leather mix. With these fixes it would be worth sending.

results.requestText: Long travel day tomorrow — I want to be comfortable but still look put-together.

looks.title: Cord and Cream
looks.idea: Warm, textured and soft all day: chocolate cord and a chunky cream knit, with the first outing for trousers you've barely worn.
looks.howToWear: Wear the fisherman jumper loose over the cords with the hem left out. Push the sleeves to the forearm. His long arms will look better with them pushed up than strained at the wrist. Wear the brown belt only if you want the waist defined. Put the navy scarf under the waxed jacket collar and tuck it in against the wind. Pack the roll-top backpack as your carry-on.
looks.why: The cords have been unused because they had no partner. Cream is the answer: ecru is in his palette, and the brown and cream pairing is the warmth he wants after living in navy and grey. The knit and cord are both soft enough for a long sit. The waxed jacket and lug-sole boots handle the showers and wet pavement, and the jacket is hip length so he can ride in it.

looks.title: Soft Tailoring, Travel Edition
looks.idea: A relaxed version of his presentation look: green merino and flannel under an unlined blazer, with boots that slip off easily at security.
looks.howToWear: Wear the green merino crew under the navy blazer with the blazer open. The grey flannel trousers sit straight over the Chelsea boots with a clean break. Use the black belt to match the boots. Add the overcoat over the top and the scarf under the lapels. If you are cycling to the station, swap the overcoat for the olive waxed jacket (d41), which is hip length and waterproof. The unlined blazer is easy to ride in and won't pull across the shoulders.
looks.why: This is a sharper version of what already works for him: the roll-neck, flannel and Chelsea combination that felt right at the presentation. The forest green merino is a colour that flatters him and gets less wear than it should. Unlined wool is comfortable for hours seated, and it looks put-together when he lands at the other end.

looks.title: Dark and Easy
looks.idea: A monochrome travel uniform in soft layers: black drawstring trousers, charcoal roll-neck and a green overshirt for texture.
looks.howToWear: Wear the charcoal roll-neck with the overshirt open over it, and the collar of the roll-neck folded down once. The drawstring trousers sit relaxed with the roll-neck left untucked. Leave the shell in the bag until the showers start, then put it on over the overshirt with the hood down. The beanie goes in the pocket for wind. Keep the white trainers for walking, since they are the most comfortable shoe he has.
looks.why: The black drawstring wool trousers are the most comfortable, flight-friendly bottoms in the wardrobe, and the wool keeps them looking smart. The roll-neck gives warmth at the neck against the wind. The forest green overshirt adds colour and brushed texture so the outfit doesn't read navy and grey. Only the shell is technical, and it works as a layer rather than a full look.

output.note: I have kept the camel suede trucker (d36) out of this: showers and suede are the reason he's avoided it, and a travel day is not the day to risk it. The rust cord shirt stays out for now, as rust sits close to his face and his bag and shoes are better handled with the quieter greens. If you tell me whether you are cycling or taking a taxi to the station, I can pick which look and outer layer suits best.

failures.detail: There is no base layer under the chunky d10 fisherman knit. On a long travel day with heated trains and cabins he needs to strip down, and he needs something softer against the skin. The d03 ecru heavyweight tee under it is the obvious finishing move and stays in the same ecru/cream story.
The d65 belt advice contradicts itself. 'Wear the hem out' and 'use the belt to define the waist' cannot both happen; the belt should simply be worn for the cords' fit, unseen.

looks.comment: This is the strongest idea in the set. It gives d26 cords their first real partner and finally answers his warmth/texture aspiration in a palette he can wear: cream at the face, navy scarf as the cool anchor, olive d41 and lug-sole d55 for showers. It needs the d03 tee underneath. The black d60 backpack is a slight off-note against the brown/olive/cream, but it's his only proper travel bag.

failures.detail: This is essentially his known presentation look (d21 flannel, d51 Chelsea, d40 overcoat) with the d12 green merino swapped in. It is reliable but adds little for a travel brief whose first word is 'comfortable'.
In the cycling swap, the d30 blazer will hang below the hip-length d41 waxed jacket. The blazer hem peeking out under a shorter coat is a messy line on a 188cm frame.

Two claims go unexplained. 'Unlined blazer is easy to ride in and won't pull across the shoulders' is asserted, not reasoned. 'Comfortable for hours seated' ignores that flannel trousers and a blazer crease badly over a long sit.

looks.comment: This is a polished, colour-correct look: green merino near the face is a good call, and slip-on d51 Chelsea boots for security is genuinely practical thinking. But it's the safest of the three and answers 'put-together' more than 'comfortable'. The overcoat is fine for a taxi, while the swap for cycling creates a hem problem.

failures.detail: d52 white leather trainers on a 6°C day of passing showers and wet pavement get soaked and stained. They are also the coldest shoe option. d51 Chelsea boots (rubber sole, slip-on at security) do the comfort job better.
Keeping the d42 shell in the bag until it rains leaves him in just an overshirt in wind at 6°C. With passing showers he will be taking it on and off all day.
The black nylon d42 shell over a boxy flannel overshirt is the least texture-led, least Lemaire/Howell outer layer available. The waterproof d41 waxed jacket does the same job in his language.
'Monochrome' is contradicted by the green overshirt. 'Fold the roll-neck down once' is filler. Calling the white trainers 'the most comfortable shoe' ignores the weather.

looks.comment: The base is right: d25 drawstring wool plus the d05 roll-neck is the most genuinely travel-comfortable pairing in the wardrobe, and the d34 overshirt adds texture. But the white trainers and technical shell drag it toward commuter-generic and fail the showers. Swap to d51 and d41 and this becomes the best look of the three.

judgement.missedOpportunity: The comfort-first look that still reads polished: d25 black wool drawstring trousers + d05 charcoal lambswool roll-neck + d34 forest green flannel overshirt + d51 black Chelsea boots (slip off at security, grip in rain) + d41 olive waxed jacket (waterproof, hip length, rideable) + d62 navy scarf + d64 watch + d60 backpack. This is Look 3 rebuilt around the drawstring waist without the white trainers and the nylon shell.
judgement.summary: This is a thoughtful set with real range and good wardrobe instincts. It brings the neglected d26 cords and d12 green merino into play, sensibly keeps the suede d36 and rust d09 out, and asks the right question about cycling versus taxi. Look 1 is a genuine idea that serves his warmth aspiration and only needs a d03 base layer and a clearer belt instruction. Look 2 is competent but leans on his existing presentation formula and trades comfort for polish; its cycling swap also creates a blazer-under-short-jacket hem problem. Look 3 has the most comfortable base but fails the weather with white trainers and a parked shell. It drifts toward technical-commuter rather than texture-led, and it shouldn't go out as written. Fix Look 3's shoes and outer layer and add the tee to Look 1, and this becomes a strong send.

results.requestText: What should I wear to work tomorrow?

looks.title: Sage Set, Undone
looks.idea: Her unworn-in-practice sage linen co-ord, softened with a white tee so it reads like a relaxed suit.
looks.howToWear: Wear the sage linen shirt open as a light jacket over the white fitted tee, with the tee half-tucked into the wide-leg trousers. Roll the sleeves to just below the elbow and leave the trousers full length so they skim the top of the slides. Keep the jewellery fine: hoops, chain and watch. Put the sunglasses on for the commute.
looks.why: Sage is one of her flattering soft cool colours, and it's head-to-toe without being loud, which suits her 'more interesting, not loud' aspiration. Linen is the right call for 24°C and humid. The set has only been worn once, and this look breaks it up so it feels easy rather than matchy. The tan slides repeat the shoe from her white-linen-and-jeans look that felt effortless.

looks.title: Cobalt, Finally
looks.idea: Her never-worn cobalt satin skirt, played down with a boxy white tee and trainers.
looks.howToWear: Tuck the front of the boxy white tee into the skirt at the waist and let the back hang loose, so the skirt sits on her slim hips. Wear it with the white trainers to keep the satin casual. Add the gold hoops and chain, and the watch. Carry the cream cardigan in your bag or over your shoulders for the air-con. For a leadership meeting, swap the trainers for the silver ballet flats.
looks.why: Cobalt is on her flattering list, and white next to her face keeps it fresh. The drape of the satin against a plain boxy tee and trainers is how she gets 'interesting' without anything fussy or costume-like. It's the minimal, easy formula she already trusts: a clean tee with one standout piece. It also finally gets the skirt worn.

looks.title: Tonal Blues, Quietly Sharp
looks.idea: Navy tailoring and soft blue in one tone-on-tone line, the grown-up version of shirt and trousers.
looks.howToWear: Tuck the front half of the light blue oversized shirt into the high-rise navy pleated trousers and add the tan belt. Leave the top button or two undone and roll the sleeves to the elbow. Keep the shirt's volume loose over the shoulders. Finish with the silver pointed flats and the watch and hoops.
looks.why: The navy trousers are her only tailored bottom, so this is the look to reach for if the day turns into a review or presentation. Navy and dusty light blue are both in her flattering palette and avoid black near her face. The wide straight leg and oversized shirt give her relaxed shapes that suit her broad shoulders and slim hips. The silver flats add a bit of interest and look polished.

output.note: Your wardrobe has no light-coloured summer tailoring beyond the navy trousers, so if you have a presentation, Look 3 is the strongest. The black blazer is the only structured layer and is too heavy for 24°C, so I've left it out.

failures.detail: The fitted tee s02 half-tucked under an open shirt into wide-leg s27 is a little fussy, and the half-tuck mostly disappears under s17. A full tuck of the boxy tee s01, or a clean full tuck of s02, would give a crisper waist line under the open shirt and suit her preference for straight, relaxed shapes.

looks.comment: This is the right instinct: she has worn the sage co-ord s17/s27 once, it is in her palette, it is linen for a humid 24°C day, and wearing it open over white breaks the matchiness while keeping the tonal line. With the tan slides s53 it is a direct cousin of her proven white-linen-and-jeans formula, but more grown-up.

failures.detail: A front-tuck of the boxy hip-length s01 into bias-cut satin s34 leaves the loose back hem bunching over a fluid skirt, and the jersey bulk at the waist breaks the drape. A full tuck, or a shorter clean hem, would let the satin fall properly.

'Cardigan over the shoulders' with s42 adds a preppy note that is off her minimal DNA. Cream against bright white s01 and s50 is also slightly unresolved. Carrying the cardigan in the bag is the better instruction.

looks.comment: This is the most interesting move in the set: the never-worn cobalt s34, played down with a white tee and trainers, is exactly the 'interesting but not loud' Toteme-style formula she asked for. The silver-flat swap for a review is smart. The execution at the waist needs tightening.

failures.detail: An oversized poplin shirt s08 kept 'loose over the shoulders' adds width to her broad shoulders. Half-tucking it into pleated high-rise s30 with a belt stacks bulk at the waist, which undercuts the 'quietly sharp' promise for a presentation day. A full tuck with the sleeves pushed up would read cleaner.
There are a lot of competing finishes: tan belt s68, black tote s60, silver flats s56, gold hoops s63 and a silver watch s65. Dropping the belt or committing to one metal would quiet it.

looks.comment: A sensible, flattering tonal-blue look built on her only tailoring, and the right call if the day steps up. It is the most conventional of the three, though, and the wool-blend s30 is borderline for a humid 24°C commute.

judgement.missedOpportunity: Cobalt skirt s34 with the white linen shirt s07, fully tucked with sleeves rolled, plus tan slides s53, tan belt s68 and gold hoops s63. Linen against satin is a better texture contrast than jersey, the shirt collar reads more grown-up for work, and it ties the new skirt directly to the outfit she already knows works.

results.requestText: Dinner with friends at a nice restaurant on Saturday night.

looks.title: Cobalt, finally worn
looks.idea: One saturated colour and a clean white top: quiet, but with real presence.
looks.howToWear: Tuck the fitted white tee in fully so the bias-cut skirt skims from the waist. Keep the hem at midi length so it moves over the silver flats. Carry the cream cardigan over your shoulders, or tie it loosely, for when the evening cools. Wear the fine gold chain and small hoops, and carry the crossbody.
looks.why: Cobalt is one of your flattering colours and the skirt has never been worn. White and cream keep it soft against your low-contrast colouring, with no black near your face. The silhouette is clean and minimal, and the satin makes it dinner-appropriate without being loud. The silver flats add a little interest and keep to your flat-shoe rule.

looks.title: Tonal blues, tailored
looks.idea: Navy and soft blue in a relaxed, grown-up suit-like mix.
looks.howToWear: Tuck the front of the oversized light blue shirt into the high-rise pleated trousers and let the back fall out slightly. Undo the top two buttons and roll the sleeves to just below the elbow. Wear the chain so it shows at the open collar. Add the black ballet flats, the silver watch and hoops, and the crossbody.
looks.why: Navy and dusty light blue sit right in your palette and read polished without effort. The wide, straight pleated trouser suits your broad shoulders and slim hips. It is the most grown-up look of the three and uses your only tailored bottom, which hasn't had much wear. It is a sharper take on your light-blue-shirt-and-jeans ease.

looks.title: Sage co-ord, dressed up
looks.idea: A soft, tonal linen set that looks deliberate rather than casual.
looks.howToWear: Wear the set as a set. Put the cream ribbed tank underneath and leave the sage shirt open and untucked, with sleeves pushed up. The tank should just skim the top of the wide-leg trousers. Let the drawstring waist sit flat under the tank. Add the tan slides, the gold chain, hoops and watch, and the crossbody.
looks.why: Sage and cream are flattering cool-soft colours, and head-to-toe tone on tone looks considered while staying easy. The linen suits a 24°C humid evening. This is a co-ord you have worn only once, and the cream tank and gold keep it from feeling like a beach set. It builds on your white-linen-shirt-and-tan-slides combination.

output.note: I left out the black strappy heels because you only wear heels to weddings. Your wardrobe has no smart flat sandal and no non-black dressy bag, so the black crossbody does the evening work in each look. If any of these feels too casual for the restaurant, swap the tan slides in look 3 for the black ballet flats.

failures.detail: s02 is the fitted tee. Sarah is most comfortable in relaxed, straight shapes, and a clingy tee over broad shoulders is not her ease. Her proven white linen shirt s07, tucked loosely into the satin with the sleeves rolled, would be more her and more grown-up.
Draping the s42 cardigan over the shoulders is a slightly fussy, preppy move. At 24°C and humid it will mostly be carried, so it adds a styling gesture rather than a real need.

looks.comment: This is the right instinct: the never-worn cobalt s34 is finally worn, with soft white at the face and the silver flats s56 giving an evening lift while respecting her flat-shoe rule. Swap s02 for s07 and drop the cardigan to make it fully hers and less studied.

failures.detail: s30 with s08 and the round-toe black flats s52 reads as leadership-review office wear. There is no evening element for a Saturday restaurant dinner.

An oversized poplin shirt s08 adds volume at the shoulders, which she already has. The half-tuck with the back hanging out is a fussy fix. A full tuck with the tan belt s68 would define the waist and give a cleaner line.
The tan belt s68 is ignored even though the pleated high-rise waist begs for it. The black nylon crossbody s61 also undercuts the tailoring.

looks.comment: This is a good-palette, very COS outfit and a sensible outing for the under-worn s30. But it is a work look borrowed for Saturday night. A full tuck, the s68 belt and a sharper shoe would carry it.

failures.detail: A linen co-ord with tan slides s53 and a nylon crossbody s61 reads as beach or holiday, not a nice restaurant. The stylist half-admits this by offering a shoe swap instead of fixing the look.

It mentions a 'drawstring waist' that s27 is not listed as having, which is a detail error. It also claims cream and gold stop this feeling like a beach set, when the slides are exactly what make it one.

looks.comment: Getting the once-worn sage set s17/s27 out is worthwhile, and the colours suit her. As sent, though, it is a resort outfit. It needs the silver pointed flats s56 rather than the slides, with the shirt worn buttoned and loosely tucked to read deliberate.

judgement.missedOpportunity: Cobalt satin skirt s34 with the white linen shirt s07, loosely tucked with the sleeves rolled. Add silver pointed flats s56, gold hoops s63, the fine chain s64 and the silver watch s65. This builds directly on her proven white-linen-shirt look, keeps the relaxed shape at the shoulders, and makes the never-worn cobalt feel effortless and grown-up for dinner.
judgement.summary: This is a thoughtful set. It deliberately activates under-worn pieces (s34, s30, s17/s27, s56), keeps black away from her face, respects the flat-shoe directive, and honestly flags that she has no dressy non-black bag. Look 1 is the strongest and nearly there; swapping the fitted tee for her proven linen shirt would make it excellent. Look 2 is polished but reads as office rather than Saturday night. Look 3 is too beachy with slides and nylon for a 'nice restaurant'. The silver flats should have been used beyond one look, as they are the wardrobe's best evening shoe for her.

results.requestText: Surprise me — put together something I wouldn't normally think of.

looks.title: Cobalt, Dressed Down
looks.idea: Satin skirt meets boxy tee and trainers, so the colour you love finally gets worn.
looks.howToWear: Tuck only the front of the boxy white tee into the skirt, so the hem sits loose at the sides and the waist stays soft. Wear the skirt at your natural waist so it falls straight from your slim hips. Finish with the clean white trainers, small gold hoops and the fine chain at the neckline. Add the silver watch, black sunglasses and the crossbody slung across the body.
looks.why: Cobalt is one of your flattering cool colours, and it puts colour near your face without any fuss. The relaxed tee and trainers keep it easy and minimal, which is how you like to dress. The satin makes the look more grown-up and interesting without being loud. It's a spin on your white-tee-and-jeans formula, with the skirt in place of the jeans.

looks.title: Sage on Sage
looks.idea: The linen co-ord split into an open overshirt and trousers, in one soft tonal wash.
looks.howToWear: Wear the sage linen shirt open and unbuttoned as a light jacket over the cream ribbed tank. Push the sleeves to the elbow and leave the hem untucked. Wear the wide-leg trousers at your waist with the drawstring tied flat, and let them skim the top of the tan slides. Add the gold hoops and fine chain, and carry the straw tote with sunglasses on.
looks.why: This is the co-ord you've only worn once, styled so it doesn't read as a matching set. Opening the shirt over cream breaks it up and adds depth, while the tonal sage keeps the look minimal. It's breathable linen for 24° humid weather. Sage and cream suit your cool, low-contrast colouring, and the tan slides echo your white-linen-shirt-and-slides look that worked.

looks.title: Blue Note Tailoring
looks.idea: Navy tailoring and dusty blue poplin with a silver flat for a quietly sharper exec day.
looks.howToWear: Tuck the oversized light blue shirt fully into the high-rise navy pleated trousers and blouse it slightly at the front. Add the tan belt through the loops. Roll the sleeves to just below the elbow and undo the top two buttons with the collar relaxed. Wear the silver pointed flats with the trouser hem just skimming the ankle. Add the gold hoops, fine chain and silver watch, and carry the black tote.
looks.why: Your only tailored bottom, paired with the light blue shirt, gives a step-up look for a leadership review without a blazer, and it avoids black near your face. Tone-on-tone blues are in the Toteme and COS spirit, and the straight, wide cut suits your broad shoulders and slim hips. The silver flat adds a small, unexpected shine that makes it more interesting while staying flat and quiet.

output.note: The brief was something unexpected, so the main surprise is the never-worn cobalt skirt, plus the sage co-ord broken up into separates. The wardrobe has no soft-coloured trousers or light bags beyond the straw tote, so black bags appear where you need a structured one.

failures.detail: Claims s34 'puts colour near your face'. It is a skirt worn at the waist, so the only colour at her face is white s01 and black sunglasses s67. Factually wrong, and it teaches the wrong lesson.

Satin-slip-skirt-plus-tee-plus-trainers is the most predictable formula for this piece. For a 'surprise me' brief it unlocks s34 but builds nothing she couldn't have guessed. The white s50 trainers keep it firmly in her comfort zone.

The black nylon crossbody s61 is the cheapest-reading bag in the wardrobe and drags the look down when the aim is 'grown-up'. Gold hoops and chain (s63, s64) plus the silver watch s65 are mixed without intent. Silver flats s56 would have tied to the satin sheen and lifted the look.

looks.comment: Right call to finally wear the never-worn cobalt s34, and it is weather-appropriate and on-DNA. But it is the textbook answer, the bag is weak, and the reasoning about colour at the face is simply wrong.

failures.detail: Wearing the s17/s27 co-ord together with a tank underneath is how the set was designed to be worn. Calling it 'split into separates' overstates the idea; it still reads as head-to-toe sage.
Says opening the shirt means it 'doesn't read as a matching set'. It still does. The real argument is the tonal sage column on a 172cm frame, which the explanation never makes.

looks.comment: A genuinely good, breathable look for 24° humidity, and it gets the once-worn sage co-ord out of the cupboard. Sage near the face suits her cool, low-contrast colouring. Pleasant rather than surprising: the cream s13, tan s53 and straw s62 make it a familiar resort recipe.

failures.detail: The brief was 'surprise me' with no occasion given. The stylist invented an exec-day brief and answered with a classic shirt-and-trousers office look, whose only surprise is the s56 flats.

The tan belt s68, black tote s60, silver flats s56, silver watch s65 and gold hoops and chain s63/s64 give five competing accent notes on a quiet two-blue base. This undoes the Toteme restraint the look claims.

An oversized poplin s08 fully tucked and bloused into pleated high-rise s30 stacks volume at the waist and widens her already broad shoulders. A half-tuck, or a tighter tuck with less blousing, would keep the line clean.

looks.comment: The navy and light-blue tonal pairing is a smart, flattering idea, and s56 is a good under-used find. But the accessories are cluttered, and it answers a brief she didn't ask for. Edit it to silver only: drop s68 and keep s65 and s56.

judgement.missedOpportunity: The genuinely unexpected look sat between Looks 1 and 2: cobalt satin skirt s34 with the sage linen shirt s17 worn open over the cream ribbed tank s13 (or loosely tucked), silver pointed ballet flats s56, silver watch s65 and the straw tote s62. Two cool, flattering colours she would never think to combine, two neglected pieces activated at once, satin against linen for texture, a flat she can wear all day, and sage linen near her face rather than black. That is 'more interesting but not loud'.
judgement.summary: Sensible and on-DNA: all three looks avoid black near the face, respect flats-only, and dig out under-worn pieces (s34, s17/s27, s30, s56). But for a 'surprise me' brief the stylist mostly reached for textbook formulas: satin skirt with tee and trainers, a co-ord worn as a co-ord, and shirt with tailored trousers. They never made the bolder cross-wardrobe pairing the brief invited. Accessorising is the weakest area: the cheap s61 crossbody, inconsistent gold and silver mixing, and a cluttered Look 3. The explanations include one plain error, about s34 adding colour near the face. Competent and wearable, but not yet the studio's standard.

results.requestText: It's raining all day and I'll be walking a lot. What should I wear?

looks.title: Sage Set Under the Trench
looks.idea: A tonal sage co-ord under the trench: calm, grown-up and cool-toned, in fabric that breathes in the humidity.
